speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
that Bill C-2, an act to amend the National Energy Board Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to begin the debate on Bill C-2, an act to amend the National Energy Board Act. As my colleagues will recall, in the budget speech of February 26 last, the then Minister of Finance, the hon. Michael Wilson, announced that the Government of Canada had made a decision to relocate the National Energy Board, or the NEB, from Ottawa to Calgary, Alberta.
The bill we are discussing in the House today is a necessary piece of work in order to facilitate that move. The bill to amend the National Energy Board Act will make it possible for the Government of Canada to follow through on those commitments and plans.
This bill and this move has to be put into some context. The National Energy Board was formed in 1959 by the then government of the late Right Hon. John Diefen-baker during the time when Canada's oil and gas industry was being organized in an attempt to make it a national economic instrument for the development of Canada, with particular interest for the producing provinces.
In 1961 the so-called first agreement on how Canada's oil and gas resources would be used in Canada was formulated. Colloquially, it became known as the Ottawa Valley line because from Canada's Pacific coast to the Ottawa Valley western Canadian oil and gas would be used for those Canadians living in that part of Canada.
That agreement had followed a very acrimonious debate, the so-called 1957 pipeline debate. The result was that when the government came into office, there was an attempt to bring about some form of order within
May 23, 1991

the industry. Equally important, there was to be an agency to allow both producers and consumers to have access to a regulatory process bringing some order to both sides of the energy equation.
I believe that agreement served Canada very well. It allowed us in western Canada to develop an industry which today is a major economic engine, not only for that region of the country, but all of Canada. If one takes a look at Canada's balance of trade payments, it is that industry which is very instrumental in Canada's economic growth and stability. Even in the most recent gulf crisis, when other countries were looking for sources of supply of oil, Canada remained in a self-sufficient position and was not asked by the International Energy Agency, for example, to develop strategic petroleum reserves, as other countries such as the United States, Germany and Japan have had to do.
Since 1961, there have been in this House a great number of debates relating to ownership of the resource and control of the resource.
Those of us who come from western Canada have always argued that the Natural Resources Transfer Act of 1930 once and for all confirmed conclusively that resource ownership lay in the hands of the provinces. I mention that as background.
Even in the early days when the National Energy Board was formed, it was argued that as a demonstration, so that the Government of Canada should have a presence throughout the country, it should be located some place other than in the national capital.
That is history. I am pleased that through this long debate this legislation is a further step in fulfilling not only the commitment made in the most recent budget speech, but the vision of the value this industry could have to Canada's future.
This move is being made for a number of very good reasons. I hardly need to remind hon. members that we live in a critical juncture in Canada's history, at a time when the forces of disunity and divergence threaten the unity of a nation that generations of men and women have toiled to build.
It is extremely important at this point in time that national policy be responsive to the aspirations of Canada's regions for a fuller participation in our national life
Government Orders
and greater proximity to the making of decisions which shape the economic future of our country.
Western Canadians in particular have increasingly felt that their problems were not always well understood in Ottawa and that decisions were sometimes taken without a full appreciation for their views and perspectives.
I could quote nothing better than the member for Edmonton-Southeast. In his book Uneasy Patriots he said, and I quote but one paragraph of which there are many I could quote.
On page 96 he said:
Defenders of the NEP -
The National Energy Program.
- agree that one of its objectives was to establish the leadership of Ottawa in the energy sector. The means chosen was a bold attempt to create a new community of energy leaders with a primary loyalty to the federal government. This group was to join industrial-financial elites in Toronto and Montreal who have historically identified closely with Ottawa because of various federal measures such as the Bank Act. The NEP was thus profoundly anti-western because until 1980 our energy industry was one of the very few sectors centred in Western Canada. It was, to many Westerners, as if a national government with no elected representation on either coast had told our east- and west-coast fisheries that they should relocate their industry decision-makers to Ottawa.
That puts it in perspective.
The more than 2000 miles between the nation's capital and the principal cities of western Canada partly explains this sense of alienation. These feelings are aggravated by the fact that decisions concerning the nature of development of western oil and gas resources are perceived to be made far removed from where they impact most heavily, namely in the west.
While many Canadians appreciate the nature of the harsh realities which govern life in western Canada-most importantly, volatile and unpredictable international grain and energy markets-it is important that this understanding be reflected in our national institutions. They must be ones in which westerners can take their place as full and equal participants.
There has been another change and that is regarding cost recovery. Obviously, when we are being asked by the industry, once it makes application to the National Energy Board, to pay for the National Energy Board's costs directly as interveners and not only as taxpayers, it is important to take another note.

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
Over 80 per cent of the National Energy Board's activities relate to oil and gas produced in western Canada. The board's decisions on these matters are of importance to all Canadians. Some petitions have indicated that and we are mindful of that fact. But the board's decisions touch upon the lives of westerners in a more direct and tangible way.
The new location for the NEB will in no way diminish the quality or direction of board decisions. The planned relocation of the board from Ottawa to Calgary, while symbolic, is more important than that. It is a demonstration of the government's desire to ensure that its institutions and decisions are seen to be responsive in areas where regional impacts are profound.
Some have alleged that moving the National Energy Board will somehow throw into question the integrity and impartiality of its decisions. The argument that a national institution such as the NEB can act in a non-partisan fashion in Ottawa and not when located elsewhere is simply, to put the best face on it, preposterous. Moreover, it is an insult. It is an insult to the intelligence of the audience, it is an insult to western Canadians, it is an insult to the board's staff and it is not worthy of those who utter it. If they have other arguments, economic or whatever, I can understand the argument, but I do not understand the impartiality argument because one could say, in reverse, if that is the case, because the board has been located in Ottawa since 1959, all its decisions have been against the interest of the industry or the west as a region.
We are saying very clearly, there might be other economic arguments, but no one can question the board's integrity.
We recognize that the National Energy Board has diverse responsibilities that extend well beyond oil and natural gas. I want to assure Canadians that the board will continue to fulfil its role as that of a truly national institution. In that regard, as the board has been doing in the past, we would like to emphasize that it will continue to conduct hearings relating to pipeline and electricity transmission routes for example in centres right across
Canada. They will be in close proximity to where the project impacts and public interests are the greatest.
Most importantly, I would like to emphasize that the integrity of the board as an arbitrator of diverse industry and consumer interest is not in question. The board will continue its mandate to regulate in the Canadian public interest fairly and effectively, taking into consideration the views of all interested parties; consumers, producers and others.
I think it is also worth mentioning that the NEB employees, as they become increasingly aware of the opportunities associated with both working and living in the Calgary area, will view the relocation favourably.
I appreciate that any change of location will bring about disruption, but the fact of the matter is that when we speak about the Public Service, we speak about it in exactly those two words; it is a service to the public and it is the service concept that has to be stressed.
The National Energy Board has taken steps, in co-operation with the Treasury Board-and I want to thank the President of the Treasury Board-many of which are precedent setting, to ensure that for these individuals, the move and transition to Calgary is as smooth as possible.
I have also had an opportunity to meet the mayor, members of the council, school boards, French speaking associations in the Calgary area and educators, and I can say, without any hesitation, that the welcome these Canadians will receive in Calgary will be second to none. I appreciate the work that has been done in the Calgary region for these people.
Some individuals, regardless of what assistance we offer, will either not be able or will choose not to relocate to Calgary. The NEB will make every possible effort, within the limits of available resources, to help these employees find alternative employment.
The board's regulatory calendar for public hearings for the rest of the year and into earlier 1992 is a heavy one. That is for reasons primarily on the gas side and pipeline proposals, as well as electricity export proposals. We are taking every necessary measure to ensure that there is no loss over the transition period in the continuity and effectiveness with which the board performs its duties.
May 23, 1991

This applies of course to both its traditional duties and those frontier lands functions which it has assumed with the dissolution of the Canada Oil and Gas Lands Administration.
To show how these things work, roughly 10 days ago the governments of the Northwest Territories and Yukon signed a memorandum of understanding for further development in the regulatory process in conjunction with the federal government's responsibility of the regulation of oil and gas, particularly north of 60.
I recall in 1979 when we were negotiating with these very people as to the future of their area, specifically on the COPE agreement. Now some 10 years later, the people who were negotiating the agreement are now ministers in those governments and they also see the need not only for regulation, but also very strongly endorse their western Canadian presence.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, the move to Calgary will offer a new chapter in the history of the NEB. That history has been one of achievement in the past. We as Canadians do not face the reality, for example, that our neighbours to the south do where roughly 50 per cent of their oil needs must be imported, while we have a self-sufficiency in oil and gas. Obviously more work has to be done in terms of frontier lands, oilsands projects, other projects such as offshore with Hibernia, LASMO and Cohasset-Panuke because the oil production in the western sedimentary basin is dropping. We knew that. Our projections were correct.
These are changes that will come in the industry. One thing I know is that as the board relocates in Calgary it will continue to offer high standards and excellent service to the Canadian public. I believe Canadians will recognize that Calgary is in fact a major energy city and this national endorsement is another affirmation of that fact.

Mr. Speaker, as the energy critic of the Official Opposition, I would indicate at the outset that the leader of my party and the party supports the spirit and letter of Bill C-2. The important issue of employer-employee relations, a subject which is not the long suit of those on the other side,

will be dealt with by my colleague from Ottawa West when she becomes the second speaker for my party.
We believe that the matter should be moved quickly to a legislative committee and there the questions of employee rights and employer responsibilities can be dealt with quickly. As you will be aware, Sir, being an Albertan yourself, the NEB has already leased space in Calgary. You and I both wish it were in Edmonton but I think as northern Albertans we recognize that unfortunately Calgary, speaking as a northern Albertan, does have the ERCB and is the more logical place to put the NEB than our own city.
Space has been leased and the move is going ahead. I think the member for Ottawa West will deal in detail with what it means to the careers, children in high school and university and a good many families of those who do not choose to go with the board to Calgary.
It should also be stressed-and I think the minister mentioned this point-that the relocation of the NEB to Calgary will save our western oil and gas industry money and make it easier to deal with a regulatory agency.
As a member from Edmonton, you will be aware, Sir, that since 1986, two years after this government came to office, approximately 50,000 bread winners in the western oil patch have lost their jobs. The industry continues to hurt badly.
At present energy company representatives have to make frequent trips to Ottawa. One of the advantages of moving the NEB to Calgary will be a reduction of the costs of coming to Ottawa and staying in expensive hotels and the like.
I might tell the minister that last night I had dinner with one of his former constituents. I have to say, without revealing any names, that I do not think that particular former constituent is going to be voting for the minister's party any more.

the NEB. Trips for the hearings are often lengthy-and I think that is an understatement-and expensive particularly since the government has made applicants pay to have their cases heard by the board to cover the costs of operation.
It is estimated that 90 per cent of the National Energy Board's operating costs, about $25 million yearly, is funded by the deeply wounded oil and gas industry from western Canada.

I congratulate the minister on his reading habits. I am glad he quoted from the book. I guess if he can quote from it, so can 1.1 am going to quote from both of them. I would like, if I may, Sir, to read-
I have them both.

Oh, you have them both. Well, why didn't the minister quote from that one too?
I would like to quote from the section of the first book Uneasy Patriots, called Oil Sands, Coal and Natural Gas.
Who is the author?

You have known him a long time, Mr. Speaker. This was written in 1988.1 know you have your copy with you this morning. A paper presented to provincial energy ministers in 1986 estimated that without new sources of supply Canada would require imports to meet one-quarter of its light crude and oil needs by 1990 and more than half by 2000.
It seems to me to follow that western Canada should aim to become the technological world leader for oil sands energy development. It would certainly help Edmonton.
A new mined oil sands project in Fort McMurray which was to start in 1996 unfortunately will not, and an upgrader at Lloydminster to start in 1993, recently
announced amid much controversy as to its economic viability and I understand viability remains a major problem for that facility, could become an important component of a prairie manufacturing base in the overall national interest. I skip down a bit and I mention that the security of the future supply is so critical that the risk appears to be warranted. The U.S. now has a strategic oil reserve of about 515 million barrels which, at $20 U.S. per barrel, represents a $10 billion investment in oil security without including carrying charges on the investment.
I have recently written to the minister on this matter so I will repeat it from the book. "Ottawa must also recognize that the oil sands sector badly needs help in other spheres. "Imaginative new research and development programs funded by Ottawa should assist the more promising of these technologies with a view to enhancing existing western strengths. World leadership with all of its spin-off in terms of exportive services should also be a goal".
This next paragraph I think the member for Edmonton East may not agree with.

"If, however, NEB does not permit exports beyond 1991," as was then a possibility, "a cost-benefit analysis by the Alberta Research Council predicts a virtual calamity for exploration and development in this important western industry and estimates that the present value of a no-export policy after 1991 for Canadian consumers because of resulting lower prices would be $8.8 billion between 1988 and 2003"-get this, Mr. Speaker-"the net present loss to Alberta producers"- your constituents and mine and many others-"alone would be $25.3 billion, making a net loss to the economies and governments of the western provinces of $18.3 billion over the period. Given the indications that large quantities of gas are still to be found within the western
May 23, 1991

provinces, it is surely in the general national interest to continue exports beyond 1991. Ottawa, or the Western Diversification Office, might usefully address this issue, if only by funding further research on the employment and other costs to the west of alternative gas exports supplies".
I promise not to quote any further from that book.
By the way, before I forget, I hope the member for Edmonton East will tell the members of the House whether he and his party support the move to Calgary and that he will correct me in his speech. The member for Edmonton East has indicated that he was "indifferent" about the move, but would not fight it. I hope he will explain that comment to 2.5 million Albertans when he gets up to speak.
A conviction shared by outer Canadians is that we are chronically under-represented in the Public Service, including Crown corporations, of our own national government. Atlantic Canadians protested this soon after Confederation. Toronto, Ottawa, Hull and Montreal together contain almost half of the more than 200,000 federal employees. I speak, Sir, as a former federal employee so I hope you will forgive me for that.
About one-third of the federal government employees live in the national capital region. In the United States the equivalent figure for Washington, D.C., is only 12 per cent. My leader, Jean Chretien, revealed during the early 1980s that only one out of seven senior executives in the federal Public Service lived outside of Ottawa and Hull.
Mr. Chretien also noted that as many as 70 per cent of the senior government policy makers in this city had little or no regional experience and as many as half of them had never worked outside Ottawa during their entire careers.
There appears to be a clear consensus now among federal mandarins that there is no such thing as a parallel career for their colleagues "in the regions". Job classifications, salaries, and a host of other factors make it clear to everyone that the best careers are the ones that begin and end in Ottawa.
In my view, there should be some real effort to recruit people from all areas of the country and there should be an equal chance for everybody, whether they are from St.

John's, Yellowknife, or Nanaimo. I will give the minister an example which I am sure will concern him. I am a former Winnipeger, Mr. Speaker, and I should confess that to you. Is it right that somebody who cannot afford to fly to Ottawa and open an apartment here does not have the same access to these jobs as somebody living in outer Canada? The member for Willowdale may not appreciate that the last poll that I saw for Calgary indicated, and appreciate that Calgary has been the most loyal Tory city in Canada for generations, that 11 per cent of Calgarians were planning to vote for the Tory Party in the next election. In Edmonton, Mr. Speaker, you may not be pleased to know, it was reported by one of your favourite newspapers, The Edmonton Sun, that the number of people planning to vote for the Tory Party in the next election was 9 per cent.
What about St. Albert?

I did not see the figures for St. Albert. The decision to move the NEB was done so hastily that there was insufficient time to include the announcement of the printed text of the ex-Minister of Finance's budget speech.
How are Ottawa's myriad agencies, departments and Crown corporations doing in an age of instant communication in providing regional leadership to our private sector? In 1989, only five out of forty of our largest or best-known national Crown corporations had their head offices outside of what I call inner-Canada; Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa. Not one of the five was in Atlantic Canada, and the five in western and northern Canada were the Canadian Wheat Board-well, they cannot veiy well put that in Ottawa-Cameco, formerly Eldorado Nuclear, in Saskatchewan, NWT Power Commission in Yellowknife, Petro-Canada in Calgary and the Canada Harbour Place in Vancouver. Five out of 40 of our largest Crown corporations are in western Canada. The other 35 are all located in either Ottawa or Montreal, none of them in Mississauga. Some seem to me to be
especially out of place, given the nature of their activities and locale of their clientele.
For example, why is the Farm Credit Corporation in Ottawa? I think it would be of interest to members from the west to know, which I was reminded of recently, that Mr. Chretien attempted to move the Farm Credit Corporation to Camrose-I see the member for Cam-rose and that area is in his seat-and it was blocked by the government which he supported in 1979-80. Mr. Chretien has also moved jobs to Sudbury. He has moved jobs to Atlantic Canada. He has been in a real sense the author of decentralization in this country.
Why, for example, does the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, the Farm Credit Corporation, Canada Ports and the Canadian Dairy Commission need to be located in Ottawa-Hull?
I share the concerns expressed by many of the 285 NEB and COGLA employees, who are very unhappy about uprooting their families in some cases. They were shocked by the announcement in the media of the move. There was no consultation with employee representatives prior to the announcement, I understand, and I hope the minister will clarify that as well. It was rather typically insensitive and arrogant of the government to notify them over television that they are going to undertake a major change in life style.
I feel they understand that very little thought or planning has gone into the move. I understand the minister's department still does not have a budget for the move, but he will tell us about that. I hope he will tell us the details of it.
Calgary may look distant and forbidding to an anglophone. For the 30 per cent of the NEB work force who speak French, I would point out that we have a 12,000-strong francophone community in Calgary. It has pledged to offer its help, and I am glad the minister spoke of that. I am told the Catholic Board of Education can accommodate all francophone families in the city's two French-language schools.
It is estimated that about half of the employees will elect to make the move, as was the case when TransCa-nada Pipelines moved its head office to Calgary from Toronto last year. Those who decide not to move will receive, as I understand according to federal policy,
May 23, 1991

priority for hiring in the Public Service. The member for Ottawa West will speak further about that, I believe.
I'll bet she will.

Might that be on the record, Mr. Speaker. The member for Crowfoot said: "I'll bet she will", and I hope the people taking notes of these things got that. It was one of the best lines I have heard from the member for Crowfoot.
Certainly some board members of the NEB and a certain percentage of the 285 employees will choose to remain in Ottawa. New staff would then have to be recruited from the producing sector in Calgary. I would point out to those opposite that there are a good many unemployed engineers and geologists and the like in Calgary, and hopefully some of these men and women will have a chance to work for the board. Some concerns have already been raised about their presumed predisposition to the producer's point of view. You know, if they go skiing up on Connor's Hill in Edmonton, they might ski with somebody who works for an oil company.
The ERCB has been in Calgary since its inception and I don't think anybody has ever accurately accused the ERCB of being a tame agency, a corrupted agency or biased in favour of the producers.
The NEB has proven to be an extraordinarily objective tribunal. It has not shown any propensity to favour a particular interest group. I think it would be very unfair for anybody to impugn the integrity of the agency by suggesting that its impartiality and even-handedness would be threatened on the basis of relocation to Calgary. It is also true that it is a move from the "corridors of power" to the capital of the oil and gas sector, one of the few to be located in western Canada. Should we question the board's impartiality? I do not think we should.
Ontario and western Canada have had their energy differences in the past, and may have again in the future.
Differences may occur-
Do you remember black Tuesday?

Yes, I do. If you are not careful, I will read from my book on that subject.
Government Orders
Differences may occur, but the location of the NEB hardly seems to justify renewed tensions. When the idea to establish some form of national energy body was first suggested to the minister, C. D. Howe, an Ontarian, snapped: "What in hell would such an agency do that I do not do already?"
The question was rhetorical. The creation of the NEB was not a sudden flash of inspiration, it was a natural progression of regulatory developments stretching back to the early 1900s.
What was new then was the fact that for the first time an independent tribunal had been established to provide advice to the federal government on certain energy matters, based on evidence put before its members at public hearings conducted in the nature of a court.
The board continued to be actively engaged in an advisory capacity because of its broad knowledge of energy matters generally, familiarity with the operation of many sectors of the industry and its involvement as a regulator with respect to many of the energy issues that came to the fore over the succeeding years.
Over a period of 32 years the scope and extent of its activities have expanded significantly, in part because of the broadening of its legislative mandate by Parliament, but even more because of the enormous growth in the scale and complexity of energy issues in which the board was involved, both as an adviser and as a regulator. It certainly stood the test of time.
I think I still have a few moments. The minister may have missed this section of the book, and I am sure the member for Mississauga missed this section of the book. As an Albertan, since much of the energy industry, oil and gas is in western Canada, I would like to say something about my own province which may even be of interest to the minister.
It reads: "The lack of western diversification does not satisfactorily explain the volatility of the Alberta economy. Why were the province's booms and busts since 1980 significantly worse than in Texas or Oklahoma, two American states with similar reliance on oil and agriculture? Why did the province experience a net loss of about 100,000 people between 1980 and 1989? During the decade, home prices collapsed; 14 provincial financial institutions failed or were forced to amalgamate; approximately one-third of the credit unions were placed under direct government supervision. The social

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
and human costs to thousands of Alberta families and individuals were enormous.".
The Calgary economist, Robert Mansell, points out that unemployment in the province did not return to its pre-1981 recession high until May 1987 compared to November 1983 for Ontario; in 1984 for Atlantic Canada; in June 1984 for Quebec.
Contrary to the conventional wisdom in Ottawa that it was the drop in oil and farm prices that caused the most severe Alberta recession since the Great Depression, Mansell notes that the average price for oil and gas producers did not decline until 1986 and farm receipts remained quite stable during the period.
By 1980, Alberta's petroleum industry accounted for almost one-third of the provincial economic output, approximately one-half of all construction starts and about 80 per cent of the province's yearly spending." I say parenthetically, Mr. Speaker, that probably about 20 per cent of your constituents and 20 per cent of my constituents, perhaps more in southeast Edmonton than in yours, are directly involved in the oil and gas industry as a way of earning their livelihood.
"The growing dependence on the oil industry made Albertans increasingly vulnerable to anything that threatened new investment in the sector, including the NEP and high interest rates. Another important factor was that by 1980, Ottawa's taxation spending and energy policies as a whole were withdrawing about $15 billion more each year than the national government was injecting into the province through all forms of federal spending.
A major consequence of this was the transfer of numerous jobs and incomes out of the province, which severely weakened the provincial economy." I skip a paragraph and this one is worth noting.
This was written in 1990: "Albertans wonder why Alberta and not our largest and richest province, Ontario, has continued between 1980 and 1988 to be the only province from which Ottawa removes more in federal taxes than it spends. Why should parts of outer Canada be the cash cows of Confederation, providing cheap inputs for the industrial heartland?" If I were writing that now I would note that Ontario was losing about 3,000 jobs a day, I understand, in the manufacturing
sector. The free trade agreement will have to be renegotiated by a new government after the next election.
While the Mulroney government continues to spend more in Ontario than it raises in federal revenues, thereby increasing inflation, his finance minister argues that sky-high interest rates are necessary to dampen inflation.
In August 1990, the Prime Minister told his constituents in Charlevoix-I do not want to speak against the Prime Minister. I will leave that part out.
Oh, oh.

Do not coax me.
Some additional data on federal spending and taxation by province released by Mansell in August 1990 were equally distressing. Between 1961 and 1988 Albertans contributed $145.7 billion. Will the member for Willow-dale tell the opposite side how many zeros there would be in $145 billion?
Almost as many as in the Conservative Party.

Expressed as 1990 dollars, it is more to Ottawa's revenues than it received in federal spending and transfers.
British Columbians were the only other net contributors to Confederation during the same period. Ontarians, who might have been expected to have contributed generously to have-not provinces, received $24 billion more in spending than it paid in taxes during the same years.
Most of the national government is located in Ontario and the argument is frequently made that this explains this anomaly. How then to explain that between 1970 and 1979 Ontario made a net contribution to residents of the other provinces of about $3.6 billion?
Mansell's latest figures also indicate that since 1980 alone, the province of Quebec has received $95 billion from Ottawa, more than it contributed to the national government.
I will spare talking about the CF-18. I would ask the minister, when he is explaining the budget, to put it on the record and tell us why the one surface mining laboratory in western Canada, that at Devon, Alberta, which had, I believe, 12 PhDs working there doing research on surface coal and who wanted to do research, as I understand it, on things like the oil sands and other important matters, was, in effect, disbanded. Why were 12 professionals who had moved in good faith from
May 23, 1991

Ottawa to Devon, Alberta, in effect told that they could get out of Alberta and go back to some other line of work? I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong. We have had a good many letters and exchanges on this. I would be grateful for his comments on that.
I guess this has been a pretty long talk. I think I have made all the points I was planning to make. I do not want to take any more time in the House. I hope it is clear to those opposite that this party, subject to what the member for Ottawa West will say, supports this move. We support decentralization.
I will end on that note.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Under the new rules the first two speakers have 40 minutes plus no questions or comments. Now we have the third speaker, the hon. member for Edmonton East, who will have 20 minutes plus 10 minutes questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, I am tempted to refrain from dispelling the tension that I am certain has gripped the House now as people anticipate on which side of the issue the New Democratic caucus will fall. It is with concern for the well-being and equanimity of my colleagues in this House that I decide at the top to inform them that the New Democratic Party, on the basis of a free vote in its caucus, will support this bill and will support the move of the National Energy Board to Calgary.
Having said that, I feel compelled to point out in a number of regards why the quote was attributed to me and noted by the hon. member for Edmonton-Southeast to the effect that the move of the Energy Board to Calgary was a matter of indifference. I did say that, but before getting into it, I would like to note that what we are dealing with here is a matter of government polity that was apparently conceived so hastily that it was shoehomed into the budget speech long after the date for the actual printing of the budget speech had passed.
This means that those of us following the finance minister's words on the written page found ourselves
Government Orders
hearing the announcement of the move without being able to read it.
This indicates, better than anything else could, the nature of the haste of the decision. Why was the decision made in haste?
Why?

I would suggest that it is because it was made on the occasion of the return to Ottawa of the Prime Minister, who previously had been in Calgary and in the west and who had discovered to his dismay that all of these nasty rumours circulating in the national capital about the collapse of the Conservative Party in western Canada were not rumours at all. They were facts.
It was resolved that something quickly must be done to address this problem. "What to do? What to do? What to do? We could alter our economic policies and bring in new policies that will be of benefit to the west but no, no, no. That would require stepping on too many important major corporate toes. What to do? What to do? What to do?"
The decision was made to move the headquarters of the National Energy Board, its board and its staff, to Calgary, the perceived hotbed of Reform Party activity, in such a way as to salvage at least a couple of seats in that city for the Conservative Party.
As the minister noted in his remarks upon moving second reading of this bill, the move is a symbolic one. "Symbolic" was the term he used, and that is correct. It is more easily understood to be correct when you consider exactly what it is we are moving and why. In this sense it is and remains a matter of indifference to me.
What now is the National Energy Board? Why, as the member for Edmonton Southeast noted, are applications for employment with the board actually declining? The National Energy Board as we find it today is little more than a pale shadow of its former self. It has every bit as many employees but its duties and the range of activities that it is charged with undertaking on behalf of the

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
Canadian people have been radically cut back, in five areas especially.
Those who have been following the energy industry for a while will remember the old concepts of security of supply and, consequently, the surplus test.
Before the passage of the free trade agreement, the National Energy Board had broad powers to regulate energy exports to ensure that they were in the Canadian public interest. Old section 119 of the NEB act gave the board the power with the approval of cabinet to: "revoke or suspend the licence if"-in the case of a licence other than a licence for the exportation of power-"the board is of the opinion that the public convenience and necessity so require."
More specifically, section 118 of the old act gave the board the power to "satisfy itself that the quantity of oil, gas or power to be exported does not exceed the surplus remaining after due allowance has been made for the reasonably foreseeable requirements for use in Canada".
This included the so-called and justly famed surplus test. Mr. Roland Priddle, the Chairman of the NEB, noted in his testimony of August 27, 1988, before the Senate Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs when it was studying Bill C-130, an act to implement the free trade agreement, in response to a question at pages 34:39 of the transcript of that hearing: "You are correct. Under the law as it presently stands, the government cannot initiate an export where the board has declined to issue a licence. So if an applicant has failed to convince the board that the gas is surplus and that public interest criteria are met, the government cannot then nevertheless grant a licence unless it took special legislative powers to do so and to override the National Energy Board."
Mr. Priddle in the same instance: "When Bill C-130",-that was the free trade act-"is enacted, unless it is amended, it would not be possible-to put the clock back and restore the application of the surplus test." "So unless the bill to implement the free trade agreement were changed, no, it would not be possible to revert to the present style or the old style of applying the surplus test".
Once again, the chairman of the committee pro tempore, the Hon. John B. Stewart asked: "Under section 83 of the present National Energy Board Act, if the board refused a licence to export, the government could not
overrule the board. Is that correct?" Mr. Priddle responded: "That is correct, Mr. Chairman".
The free trade agreement did away with the surplus test. Annex 905.2 of the agreement contains the following provision:
It is understood that the implementation of this Chapter includes
the administration of any "surplus tests" on the export of any energy
good to the other Party in a manner consistent with the provisions of
Articles 902, 903 and 904.
That was the specific elimination of the so-called surplus test.
After the amendments to the National Energy Board Act were made as result of the Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act in December 1988, the NEB was ordered to give effect to the agreement in new section
119.2	of the act. The cabinet, instead of the NEB, was given the power to restrict exports, and then only if the FTA provisions were not violated. That is in new section
119.3	of the act. The NEB can only suspend its determination for granting an export licence for 120 days. However, even before the 120 days are up, if the minister or the cabinet disagrees, the NEB is to issue the licence in question with all due haste. That is in new section
119.6	of the act.
To make it even more specific, the NEB cannot violate article 904(a), (b) or (c) of the free trade agreement. That is provided in section 119.5 of the new act. It is clear from the free trade agreement that the old surplus test is gone, an entire area of NEB jurisdiction wiped away.
Second, with regard to price determination, the board has suffered another major chop. Under the old National Energy Board Act, the board had the power, and I quote from Section 118(b) of the old act:
-to satisfy itself that thepricetobe charged for power exported-is just and reasonable in relation to the public interest-
And under section 120(2) of the old act the cabinet could set the export price or range of prices for oil and gas. These provisions were not deleted by the free trade amendments to the NEB Act, but the free trade agreement itself supersedes them. Specifically, new section 120(2) of the NEB Act allows cabinet to exempt oil and gas exported to the U.S. from any price regulations. More important, article 904(b) of the free trade agree-
May 23, 1991

ment prohibits the maintenance of export prices higher than domestic prices. Price discrimination is gone.
Do not forget, Mr. Speaker, that article 409 of the free trade agreement ensures that the proportion of exports does not fall below the previous 36-month average-the so-called free trade ratchet that requires us to continue to sell energy to the United States in a proportion of production not less than that which we exported in the previous three years. Again no higher export price can be charged.
The third big cut is the elimination of the so-called least cost alternative test. Under section 6(2)(z)(iii) of the NEB Part VI regulations-this took some research, Mr. Speaker-the National Energy Board required applicants for exports to demonstrate that the export price "would not result in prices in the country to which the power is exported being materially less than the least cost alternative for power and energy at the same location within that country".
This was one of three price tests the board established in 1967 to ensure that exporters should seek full market value for Canada's energy exports, especially in cases where there were non-arm's length transactions; discounts to penetrate new markets or to take a greater market share from other Canadian exporters, or, third, to dispel accusations of unfair trade.
On September 2, 1986, then energy minister Marcel Masse instructed the National Energy Board to review changes that could be made to simplify and reduce the regulation of electricity exports. This report was to include a review of the appropriateness of the existing three price criteria used to assess proposed electricity exports.
What do you suppose happened, Mr. Speaker? The National Energy Board conducted the review as requested stating that "the third price guideline may be a dispensable element of electricity export regulation". It added that if the guideline were deleted "the benefits accorded the bargaining position of a Canadian utility by dint of the existence and federal application of the third price guideline would be forgone". [DOT]
Government Orders
Canada agreed to eliminate the least cost alternative test for the export of energy goods in the free trade agreement in annex 905.2.
The fourth cut was contained in Bill C-23, the elimination of public hearings for most electricity export applications. Cabinet, not the NEB, now makes the final decision. The passage of Bill C-23 last session means that most electricity export applications and applications for international power lines will now not require that a public hearing be held. This used to be an important part of the NEB's job, but no more.
The final decision on whether a public hearing is held is no longer made by the NEB, it is made by cabinet. In other words, the cabinet can overrule a decision by the NEB that a public hearing should be held. This politicizes the process and seriously undermines the authority of the NEB, as we argued at the time, but that is the case. That is the fourth cut.
Fifth, and most recent, is the elimination of the market-based procedure, including the benefit cost analysis to assess natural gas export licence applications.
Price controls were eliminated by this government in the name of deregulation in 1984 and 1986. The volume-based surplus tests, as I noted earlier, were eliminated. This left the NEB relying solely on the so-called market-based procedure to assess the national interest of natural gas exports.
This procedure, briefly stated, is a complaints process where Canadian users are assured supplies of gas on conditions as favourable as export proposals. It includes an assessment of the impact of export proposals on Canadian natural gas exports, and a determination of whether proposed exports are in the national interest.
This market-based procedure, including the benefit-cost methodology used to assess natural gas export licence applications, was one of the few regulatory mechanisms that remained to protect the public interest of Canadians.
The elimination of the NEB's benefit-cost analysis sanctioned, indeed it invited, a situation in which exports of a finite, strategic commodity could result in net harm to Canada.
Even the Government of Alberta, that staunch advocate of free market ideology, recognized and made That is from pages 1, 34 and 35 of the Regulation of adjustments for the shortcomings of the natural gas Electricity Exports, a document published by the NEB in market. It blocked attempts by home owners, hospitals, June 1987.	school boards and other core natural gas users in Ontario

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
to purchase Alberta natural gas at deep discount prices, arguing that these short-term sales were not in the interest of Albertans.
However, what the Alberta government stood up for in its own interest has now been abandoned, with regard to the rest of Canada, in terms of effective regulation by the NEB. This happened, under pressure from the industry and the government, on March 15,1990, a little more than a year ago.
In its decision to abandon the market-based procedure, the NEB stated that it will: "Henceforth, not require applicants for licences pursuant to part 6 of the act to provide evidence on the net social benefits of their projects."
In short, as we pointed out at the time, this means the NEB has no effective way to block exports of finite, strategic resources even if these exports result in net harm to Canada.
As I said at the outset, the NEB is but a pale shadow of what once it was. Proof of this is the recent decision by the NEB to allow completely TCPL's application for rolled-in tolling on the building of the new pipeline to the northeastern United States, a pipeline that will be paid for by Ontario consumers. That decision was made before the board was moved to Calgary. That decision was made when the board was still right here in Ottawa.
What of intervener funding? What of funding to be supplied to those who would appear before the NEB regardless of where it is, especially as the NEB has been given new authorities to conduct environmental assessments under the so-called EARP guidelines? That, too, is still not there. The location of the NEB is, in that sense at least, a matter of indifference to me because the NEB is no longer allowed to do the job it was originally created to do.
However, I do support the move of the NEB to Calgary anyway, for three reasons.
My first reason is that, as the minister himself pointed out, over 80 per cent of the NEB's activities now relate to the oil and gas industry.
Second, in Alberta there is academic, industrial, consumer and environmentalist expertise that will be of tremendous use to the board in its assessments.
Third, it is long past time that this government started paying attention, real attention, to the concerns of the west, and not just at the symbolic level.
I will be dealing with a concrete matter in this regard during the oral question period this afternoon.
There remains only to note the concerns of the employees of the board and of the Public Service at the way in which this entire matter has been handled.
My time has expired, Mr. Speaker. I acknowledge that. However, my colleague from Nanaimo-Cowichan will, when the speaking order comes around to him, deal thoroughly with those concerns. Those concerns which we hope will be effectively addressed by the government were all that stood in the way of the New Democratic Party supporting the move of the NEB to Calgary.
We believe, on the basis of a conversation I and others, including the member for Nanaimo-Cowichan, have had with members of the Public Service and with Mr. Roland Priddle, the chairman of the board, that adequate provision will be made for those employees. Therefore it is with some considerable pleasure that I tell the House that the New Democratic Party will support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments on Bill C-2, which proposes to transfer the National Energy Board to Calgary. Obviously, I am concerned to see jobs leaving the National Capital region, especially since this seems to be a political decision and a very partisan one at that.
Whether it is better to centralize or decentralize is an issue that I would prefer to debate in the legislative committee. What concerns me most today is the problems this will cause for employees in the National Capital region, for instance loss of jobs, and also the way they were treated. The minister told us that he spoke to the municipal authorities in Calgary and the school boards, and that the people of Calgary would roll out the welcome mat. I am sure they will, and I am sure the same applies to high schools and elementary schools, because

these jobs are coming to Calgary. I am not worried about that, but I am worried about the following: How will families from the National Capital Region be treated? How were these families treated by the Department?
Mr. Speaker, I expect no one likes to hear the news on television or read it in the paper that his employer is going to transfer him-whether he is willing or not-a thousand miles from his present residence. I am worried about the francophone community in Ottawa. I am worried about anglophone and francophone communities in the national capital region that will be uprooted, because both husband and wife work to pay off the mortgage on their house. Will they have any guarantees that their spouse will get a job as well?
If we assume that the wife works for the National Energy Board, is her husband guaranteed a job? The department says it will help people look for jobs, but the minister told us earlier that there was quite a bit of unemployment in Calgaiy. Won't they have a problem here? Who will be given preference, the spouses of employees who will be transferred to Calgary or Calgary residents?
This is an interesting question. Among the families which will have to move there are certainly children who will have to change school systems since they are different from one province to the other.
The difference is even greater for francophones. I understand two French-speaking schools are prepared to accomodate them. But will they be integrated into the catholic or public school system? Will the families have a choice between the two systems? What kind of future is in store for these children? It is certainly a concern.
I very much regret this way of dealing with these families, hurrying them like that and suddenly disrupting their life in the national capital region, the life of professional civil servants. That is what concerns me the most, Mr. Speaker: the families of the civil servants being transfered.
What are their chances of finding a job? What are their chances of development in a new setting, far away from the capital? What guarantees will the government give to help these people not only to look for schools and
Government Orders
jobs but also to find schools and jobs to ensure the future of the entire family?

Mr. Speaker, I cannot speak for the board or the department with regard to the adjustment provisions that are being made for the employees, but I can at least set the hon. member's mind at ease in this regard. In terms of the amenities, educational opportunities and business opportunities that are available and in terms of the spectacular scenery and environmental wonder surrounding it, the city of Calgary is second to but one city in all of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to rise to make a comment. The member for Edmonton East deserves tremendous congratulations from this House and from the people of Alberta for the persuasive role he has played in drawing attention to the need to have some serious decentralization of policy in this country, as symbolized by this move of the National Energy Board to Calgary.
He was particularly persuasive in our caucus and has persuaded us that we, from all parts of Canada, should be supporting this move. We have our concerns about the way in which the workers here will be treated. We have received some assurances and we would hope that when this bill comes before the committee, there will be an opportunity for those concerns to be given a full airing and to be sure that they are met.
We support fully the idea that it is important that the west have the headquarters of the National Energy Board, that it be centred there. Alberta is the obvious place for it.
The member for Edmonton East has shown great leadership on this and I would like to congratulate him. I ask him if he would like to focus for a minute or two on the workers and how they might be treated in this shift. It is important, both from the point of view of the employees here and, of course, in Calgaiy, and how the workers would be received in that city.

Mr. Speaker, again I will attempt to be brief. First of all, I would like to thank the hon. member for those generous remarks. I will attempt to give them as wide as possible distribution in my riding.
With regard to the question of the employees, I would note that I have had discussions in this regard with the chairman of the National Energy Board. I know that my colleague, the member for Nanaimo-Cowichan, who will be speaking directly to this question a little later in this debate has met with representatives of the em-

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
ployees and, indeed, directly with employees. The two of us are satisfied that the adjustment package put together is a generous one. However, there are still elements in which it must be further fine-tuned. We look forward to getting the bill before committee to address that question.
There is no question that the manner in which the employees were notified was shameful. It was tawdry. It is a wrong that I do not suppose any adjustment package, however generous, could ever set right.
On the whole, we do not believe that the treatment being accorded the employees of the board is sufficiently poor to warrant opposition to the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise to speak on this bill. I know the government had hoped of having it go through with virtually no debate to escape any examination, in fact to even escape the bill being referred to a legislative committee where witnesses could be heard and the concerns of employees could be raised, along with any other matters that people might want to bring to the attention of Parliament.
However, we have made sure that that does not happen. We are insisting on it going to a legislative committee because we think there are issues that need to be addressed.
This was an extremely sudden decision of the government, an extremely sudden announcement that did not appear in the budget speech and seemed to roll off the top of the head of the Minister of Finance, as so many other things seem to have done from time to time.
That decision, with so little planning going into it, created great unfairness, threw 300 families into turmoil and in fact threatened to disrupt the operations of the board. It had not been looked at. It had not been examined, as this kind of decision would normally be. Planning had not been done for it and a schedule and so on set out.
We see some problems in the way the employees are being treated and these need to be addressed. That is why this bill must go to committee. That is why we need to hear from people who are affected by this move and to address some of their concerns.
It is evident, given the way in which it was announced and the way in which it is proceeding post-haste, that the timing is dictated more by the political agenda of the government than concern for the operation of the board or the lives of its employees and their families. I would like to give several examples.
The treatment of the employees in this case has been arrogant and insensitive in the extreme. There is nothing like finding out that your whole life is going to change, your whole career is going to be disrupted and your whole family is going to be disrupted on television at night. That is the way the employees of the board found out that their employer was moving and either asking them to go with it or leaving them behind.
A week before the budget announcement, a large number of employees were transferred into the National Energy Board but were given no hint, no indication that accepting that transfer into the board would mean a major move more than half way across the country for their families.
The government is playing with words in attempting to deprive employees of rights they are entitled to under their contract and under government policy by insisting on calling this a relocation and not a decentralization. This deprives the employees of entitlement that they are entitled to: entitlement to notice with time to plan their lives, time to plan their careers and time to work other family responsibilities around a reasonable and rational adjustment to the requirements of their employer. The decentralization policy, that is, moving a work unit-and I doubt that anybody would call this anything else-requires a normal notice period of one year. It is clear that the employees have been given a matter of weeks, not a matter of months to make a serious decision.
In rushing the move, the government is causing undue and unnecessary hardship for employees and eventually for the board. As late as April 4, employees were told not to even list their homes with a realtor, even though they were being asked to decide just four weeks later whether they would be moving to Calgary or not. Employees were told at the same time that information on the relocation package would not be available until the end of April, and at that time their decision had to be made by the middle of May. This, I understand, has now been
May 23, 1991

extended to the end of May but it is still unfair to give employees who have been loyal and hard-working, who have made the board what it is, a matter of a few days and weeks to make a major decision like this about their lives.
The government suggests that families with school-age children should relocate before September 1, but only a token portion of the board's operation will even be in Calgary by then. What will these employees be relocating to? It is not until the end of October that the major component of the board will be up and operational in Calgary, if the government's plans go ahead on schedule.
Employees are faced with deciding this week. But it will be five months before most of the board's operations will move. Now I ask the government, why is it so crucial that employees make decisions within a matter of weeks? Why does it consider that employees need only a matter of days and weeks to make this kind of decision, when the government needs at least three to five months' notice to make its moves?
Employees are asking what is the rush when this move has been under consideration on and off for nearly two decades. Surely it is possible to plan in a way that is humane to workers and humane to their families and to the other obligations they have in their communities, and still accomplish the government's objective.
Mr. Speaker, there is serious concern about discriminatory treatment, about some employees being treated as elite employees who are important to the board and others being treated as unimportant employees to the board. We have some employees being offered red carpet and expensive treatment because the board needs to keep them, and others not being offered similar treatment. Similarly, we have very special and very expensive packages for people who are moving, but no equally special consideration for those who, for one reason or another, cannot move with the board. This is not the discriminatory and unequal kind of treatment that these employees or any other employee of the government deserve.
It started within hours of the announcement, when the government hired Decima to design a package that would entice employees to relocate. The proposal from Decima made it clear that out of the 350 employees of
Government Orders
the board, their job was to put together a package that was acceptable to 35 employees. They did not want the employees to know this, so their survey scheme was going to include twice that many so that nobody would know they were targeting a special 35 people with special and discriminatory treatment.
Do we have an elite in the National Energy Board? Do we have some people who are more valuable employees than others and deserve to be treated more generously?
I don't think that is the kind of Public Service we want.
Let me give you an example. We are told head-hunting services will be provided for the spouses who relocate with an employee. The same opportunity, the same treatment will not be given to employees who stay, they will be subject only to the normal workforce adjustment policy-and there is even some question about that. We question whether this head-hunting service is only available to certain employees' spouses and whether it is a simple employment counselling service that is available to the rest of the spouses who are not one of the select 35.
Those who relocate will be reimbursed if they take an exploratory trip to Calgary to find out whether they would like to live there. But those who decide not to relocate will not get reimbursed for those expenses. Is that fair? Is that equitable? I don't think so.
Mr. Speaker, the legislation for the space agency and for the Canadian Centre for Management Development contained special provisions for employees to ensure that they were not disadvantaged, whether or not they went with the new agency. Why does this bill contain no mention of the employees, no mention of provisions for them?
The government will say that employees are subject to the normal work force adjustment policy which gives them priority for other appointments within the Public Service for a limited period of time. In fact, that policy expired on March 31. It has been extended to June 30, but just until June 30.
The employees want to know, and I want to know, what happens to them after that? What about the employees who have worked their way up to senior positions but do not have the paper qualifications for similar positions elsewhere in the government? Perhaps the minister might want to answer this. Has the NEB asked the whole Department of Energy, Mines and

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
Resources to assist in relocating these people and ensuring that they are employed.
What about people with highly specialized skills who, for one reason or another, cannot go to Calgary, much as they might like to? These are the people that the work force adjustment policy is far too limited to serve well. They are too specialized, they have become specialized in serving the Government of Canada, and therefore are less employable by other employers.
Where is the head-hunting help for these people? Where is the help for these people to find alternative employment? What about employees who are close to retirement? The government has all kinds of money to convince people to go to Calgary. What is it doing for people who are staying here? This is not their decision. They should not be the ones to suffer for it. Are we going to throw somebody out on the street without a job, a year from retirement, and make no special provisions for that person? I would hope not. These are certainly questions that need to be addressed at committee.
The government might say: "Well, that is peoples' choice. If they do not want to come with us, tough luck". I do not think that is a good policy for any employer, public or private. It ignores totally the fact that many people are unable to relocate. Often, the people who are unable to relocate are women. They may have a spouse who is the higher income earner and it does not make any sense for the family-and people do consider their families in these decisions- to uproot because of one spouse's job.
Many, and most of them are women, now have custody arrangements which prohibit them from leaving a certain region without going back to court, and that can take a long time and may not even be possible. Many have the care of elderly parents or other family or community obligations as a result they simply cannot pick up and move in a very short time frame, as is happening in this case.
What about those who decide to relocate and then cannot for one reason or another, and it may be any of the above, it may be illness or anything? These people will be considered to have abandoned their positions. In other words, they will be out of a job overnight.
The move is creating particular problems for francophones, many of whom have spouses who are not bilingual. I know the department has offered language training to those spouses. However, the plain fact is that to move to another community without a milieu that is familiar to you in your own language, your traditional connections to your culture and heritage and language, is more difficult for a francophone family in this case than it is for an anglophone family. I think the government has to pay special attention to that.
The National Energy Board has now indicated that it intends to apply for special employer status. One reason is to allow for higher rates of compensation than it now pays its employees in the government.
For many of its employees the board will have to pay up to $15,000 a year more in a location where it is competing with the private sector in the resource industry. Many employees will have to be paid that much more, or they simply will walk across the street and take a job in industry.
This special employer status has certain implications for the employee. They are not terribly clear as to what those implications are, and they are certainly entitled to know.
Does this, for instance, let the board pay support staff, who earn less, at lower rates if it allows it to pay some employees at higher rates? What assurances do these employees at lower rates have that their salary level will be protected? How does this affect those who go to Calgary and then decide to return two years from now if they are with a separate employer as opposed to their current status with the National Energy Board?
The employees have talked to me about their concern about the impact on operations of the board as well. Consultants say the normal rate of relocation for private sector moves in a case like this is approximately 50 per cent. That obviously must have a serious impact on the board's operations because the government has left very little time to make plans to ensure that there can be a smooth transition.
As a result of the political "symbology", as the minister calls it, of this move, the board itself but not most of its employees will be moving to Calgary on
May 23, 1991

September 1. In fact the board will not be fully operational until the end of October. That seems to me to create quite a little gap.
I want to address very briefly concerns raised by others, as the minister has done this morning. The minister has received letters from, among others: Consumers Gas, Union Gas, the Industrial Gas Users Association, and the Ontario Natural Gas Association. They all opposed this move and raised some very serious concerns about it.
While the minister has attempted to calm these concerns this morning, certainly one of the letters suggested specific amendments to the act that would relieve concerns about the neutrality of the board, its impartiality.
The minister's statements this morning-I take them at their word-are not helpful when spokespersons for the industry in Calgary start saying: "Won't it be nice when our kids are going to the same schools and we are skiing at the same ski hills and the board is more sensitive to the needs of the producers?"
It is not helpful when the Calgary Chamber of Commerce says that the board will be closer to its principal clients. I hope the minister is aware that its principal clients are the public. Its principal duty is to the public interest, not the producers, not the shippers or the exporters.
Consumers Gas has asked for a specific provision in the act with respect to public interest.
The concerns are exacerbated because this move coincides with the board becoming financially self-sufficient, that is funded by the industry. In fact we know the ultimate cost is to the consumer and not to the industry. Suggestions have already been made by the Canadian Petroleum Association and the Independent Petroleum Association that producers should have more control over the operations and the policies of the board.
Concerns about the public interest are legitimate and need to be addressed in legislative committee.
I want to say simply that the board reports to Parliament. It co-ordinates with many departments and agencies, even more so now that it has responsibility, beyond what it thought, for the environment.
The board has maintained an office in Calgary continually. Has the government considered whether, for purposes of parliamentary liaison and efficiency in liai-
Govemment Orders
son with other government departments, it should now maintain a smaller Ottawa office as well?
It is important for the employer and for the operation of the board that this move be carried out providing employees with every opportunity to make a decision to stay with the board. That is why we want to see some of these issues addressed. That is why we want to look at the schedule for this to see if it really makes sense to say employees have this week to decide and then stretch the move out over five months. Can we look at another schedule that is better for the board, better for the employees, and better for the public interest?

Mr. Speaker, I have just a couple of quick comments and then a specific question for the hon. member.
My first comment is that there may be members in this House who will not sense the extent to which this is important to Alberta or, as it might be, important to the province of Saskatchewan. But we are two provinces unique in the development of this country. Constitutionally we stood apart and different from all other provinces.
When Canada was formed in 1867, the presumption of resource ownership belonged to the four original provinces. It belonged to Prince Edward Island a year later, in 1868, when it became a province; likewise to Manitoba and to British Columbia.
However, in 1905, when the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan became part of Canada, the federal government kept from those provinces the ownership of natural resources. For 30 years the province of Alberta never raised enough money in taxes to be able to pay for schools and hospitals. They indebted themselves every year. For 30 years they fought, until 1930 when they won the Natural Resources Transfer Act.
Ingrained in an Alberta or Saskatchewan person is that deep resentment that somehow the federal government had coveted unto itself the resources of only two parts of Canada, where there were provincial ownerships in all other cases. It is more than symbolic. It is extremely important to those two western provinces for all of its right reasons and its symbolic reasons.
I want to ask a question of the hon. member for Ottawa West. I note that she said there are persons who had worked their way up and she had concerns for them. There are persons close to retirement and she had concerns for them. There are many who are lower income spouses, and again she expressed concerns as a

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
good member of Parliament representing constituents of hers who by and large are public servants. I commend her for the compassion she is showing.
The real question is when a move in the public interest ought to be made. That argument could be put for every move to every locale and every situation.
I just want to ask her specifically: Is she or is she not in favour of moving the National Energy Board from Ottawa to Calgary?

The member was not listening very carefully to my speech. I said I had concerns I wanted to address. I think we all recognize in this House, and I certainly do, the importance of government services being available to people across this country.
The member is obviously unaware that 70 per cent of the Public Service is not in the national capital region but is decentralized across this country. Only 20 per cent of the jobs in this community are Public Service jobs. It would be nice if before he got up he knew what he was talking about.
I also want to point out to him that he mentioned Alberta and Saskatchewan. He forgot to mention that Manitoba was formed as a province in 1870 and did not get control of its resources until 1930.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: It was 60 years.
The minister is right.
Do you favour the move?
We want to see this bill go to committee so we can see those concerns addressed. I would like to be able to support this bill whole-heartedly.

Mr. Speaker, one of the questions raised by the member for Ottawa West concerned a suggestion which was put forward in a letter to me by companies like Union Gas, that if we shift a regulatory agency such as this from Ottawa to Calgary, in this case, somehow this would represent a process of tying the agency more closely to the producer side of the industry.
I must say I find that a very strange argument. I do not see why an agency's location should affect what it is able to do in terms of justly and carefully considering questions which come before it. That is one of the reasons for some of the concerns of our caucus with respect to the workers being affected by this which we intend to take up in committee.
Nevertheless we felt that it was possible to have precisely the same kind of careful, judicious analysis of questions that come before the National Energy Board in Calgary as in Ottawa. It would seem to me that to suggest otherwise is to say there is something about the air in Calgary that destroys the capacity of people to be judicious and impartial, and that is certainly not the case.
I would therefore ask the member for Ottawa West if she would be prepared to make quite clear that she was not putting forward any suggestion that a shift of the National Energy Board from Ottawa to Calgary would lead to any change in the impartiality and the judiciousness with which that board has operated in the past and will operate in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest the member might have listened to what I was saying. I was referring to correspondence from people who have expressed legitimate concerns about this particular aspect and have asked the government to take particular steps to ensure that that does not happen. I think the board has always recognized that it was important to keep an office in Calgary-this is nothing new-to keep contact with the oil industry, and it has done that well over the years.
I would not for a moment suggest that the board would do anything but fulfil its mandate under the act and act in the best interests of the people of Canada.
None the less I think it is very important that with this bill before committee, the committee also address the concerns that have been raised by significant interests in the energy field. I repeat the point I made during my speech that if the board has always felt it important to keep an office in Calgary to be close to the producing industries, perhaps the government should now consider that it might also be important to keep an office in Ottawa since the board does report to Parliament and does work very closely with many other government departments.

Mr. Speaker, earlier today I presented a bundle of petitions, some 2,500 names, all expressing concern about this
May 23, 1991

move and signing the petitions in opposition to the move of the National Energy Board to Calgary.
I have another group of petitions with some 300 names. Most are from the Ottawa area, but some names are from different communities in Quebec, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan. I suggest that they are doing so in part because they just do not know enough about the way in which the whole thing is being handled to this point in time. New Democrats have always supported decentralization, to the best of my knowledge, if it is done in an orderly manner. We are mainly concerned about the way in which the employees are handled. Certainly in this case there is no question, and others have commented on this, that the employees were handled very badly, including the chairman of the National Energy Board himself who put up a notice in the board office to the effect that he knew nothing at all about the move other than what he had heard when the budget speech was read.
The minister of energy in presenting and speaking first on the bill said that it was in the budget speech. Technically it was because the budget speech is what the minister said in the House. Certainly we all know it was not in the printed material which was made available to the minister for his speech when he was presenting it or in the material that was distributed since, other than Hansard, which is the budget speech.
That is how the chairman of National Energy Board found out about the move according to him, and to this point we have no reason for doubting it. If he did not know then certainly the employees did not know. Perhaps even the Minister of Finance did not know, except that he got a note before he got on his feet asking him to announce this.
Why was it done in the budget speech? To the best of my knowledge it is not a budget item. Why did it have to be done then? If it were going to be kept secret from everyone the excuse could be that it was a budget matter, it was in the budget speech, but we know it was not in the budget speech until moments before the minister stood up to speak. There was no reason for the secrecy, for not letting people know if the decision was actually made earlier than the budget speech which was presented some day late in February.
