Why has everyone concerned with this move been treated so shabbily as to tell them with so little notice what was going to happen? From the start the employees
Government Orders
have been handled badly and that is the nature of our concern about this legislation.
If it were in the budget speech one would expect to find some reference to the cost. I would suggest if one read through the budget speech very carefully one would look in vain to find any reference to what it is going to cost. I have heard figures running anywhere from $40 million to $70 million. Who knows? Nevertheless it is happening. It is happening in a real hurry. That the means the cost of finding the accommodation in Calgary will probably be higher than it might have been had the government had the time to look with some care. The cost of abandoning space in Ottawa itself may be high. We do not know. Certainly the government has given every indication of downsizing. It would seem unlikely that the space currently filled in Ottawa is going to be filled with other employees unless they are spread more thinly.
The loss of expertise has been commented on. One does not know how much. How can we know? The employees had originally until the middle of May to make up their minds. They now have until the end of May to decide and only then will we know just how many will be lost and also the loss of expertise. That is a real question. Estimates have suggested that some 50 per cent of the staff will be unable or unwilling to move or a combination of both. People with families may find that they are quite unable to move, especially if there are two income earners in the family. If one has other employment here in Ottawa it is going to be very difficult for the two of them to pull up stakes along with their family and move to Calgary and it is not quite as difficult perhaps for them to stay here.
It is going to present a problem. People who have been working for the National Energy Board for some time probably have accumulated a lot of pension time and were looking forward to working for the National Energy Board until they retire. Now all of a sudden they have to deal with a situation in which their work is going to be moved some several thousand miles away from its present location and with very short notice.
In filling the vacancies, the government has been reassured by the Chamber of Commerce, according to a letter that went to the then minister of energy, I believe, that there would be plenty of expert employees in the oil industry available and willing to fill in the vacancies in the National Energy Board. I expect they would be

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
willing. If they are unemployed right now they would be even more whiling.
Unfortunately, that lends weight to the argument that they are going to be more under the influence of the oil industry in that location than they would be here in Ottawa. I think it is important that the NEB be able to do everything possible to convince people that this is not the way the system is working. I expect the National Energy Board will be very much aware of that and will be watching that carefully.
I have talked to employees' representatives and I have talked one of the employees and will be talking to more. I am pleased that this matter is going to be referred to a legislative committee so that there will be an opportunity to get in to more of the details.
One of the questions that I and others have asked is why does it have to be by the end of the September? Originally, I think it was September 1 and now it is the end of September. I do not know why it has to be that soon. Why could the government not have taken more time? Would it not have served its political purposes at least to have said: "Yes, it is happening. It is going to happen. We are going to be there a year from now or some such date"? That would have given everyone, the board itself and the employees, much more time to make their preparations and decisions. It seems to me that could have been done and it could still be done. I do not know what the magic is about the current date of September 30. If it is going to have an affect by then the deadline given to the employees has to be real because the board has to know who it is going to have working for it when it arrives in the Calgary office and opens shop.
I do not think anyone is really complaining about the special provisions enabling employees to make the move with minimum cost to themselves, at least in terms of dollars and cents. The guarantee that employees leaving Ottawa will get at least market value for their homes is a good one but even then there is so little time to make that decision, even with the deadline being extended last Friday.
The employees are going to have to sign up for two years if they are going to move to Calgary, but any time in the third year or between the end of the second and
the end of the third year they can change their mind and decide they made a mistake in going to Calgary. I do not know if it is clear whether the board would move them back to Ottawa or move them wherever they wanted to go. I have not been able to determine that yet because I just have not had a chance to read all the material.
It is tough to decide in a couple of weeks whether you are going to accept today's current market value for your home or wait and perhaps think that maybe in six months the market is going to improve and you may receive a higher amount. Why do they have to decide at the same time as they are moving? Why not give them that two or three year period to make the decision as to whether they would dispose of their homes here in Ottawa?
For all I know there may be more in the agreement than I am aware of but my understanding now is that they have to make up their minds as to whether they are going to accept the board's offer of getting minimum market value for their home at the same time as they decide whether they are going to Calgaiy.
I see no reason for that deadline not being extended, even if the government decides that it cannot do anything about the September 30 deadline for opening up shop in Calgary.
There will be opportunity now that we are going to committee and certainly we are co-operating fully. All the opposition members, as far as I know, are co-operating in getting this bill to committee because we believe that is where we can best hear from the people who are being affected. The employees are the ones I am particularly concerned about at the moment but there are others who are being affected by this, such as the industry itself. I am sure the oil industry will want to make representations as to what a great idea it is, the oil industry from Calgary anyway. It may be that user industries and other energy groups will want to make representations of their own. I am looking forward to this bill being referred to the special legislative committee, getting answers, we hope, to some of the questions and perhaps getting some movement from the government on the deadlines it has imposed, deadlines that are totally unfair to employees who heard about this from someone who heard it in the budget speech.
May 23, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
I will be very brief.
I have a question for my hon. friend and it is based on what I have seen in my 12 years here. I know that the federal government is often accused of being centralist in its attitudes and approaches and this bill is an effort to take the National Energy Board to the place where the action is. In other words, since most the people dealing with the National Energy Board are from the western provinces we should make it easy for them.
I have a question and then I have a comment. There seems to be, perhaps organized by the hon. member for Edmonton Southeast, a complaint here from people in the the west that we are moving this National Energy Board to Calgary. As a central Canadian I have great difficulty in understanding why members from the west, such as the hon. member who just spoke, are concerned about us taking this western operation out to Calgary. It seems to me to make good sense. I do not understand why the Liberals and the NDP are fighting this effort by the government to take it to the west.
That is my question. If I may reach back into my past as the housing spokesman for our party back in 1981, and having followed it ever since, I can say that one should never worry about the prices of houses in Ottawa; they do not go up, they do not go down and they do not follow the trends of any other city in the country. This place is recession-proof. I do not understand why the member for Edmonton Southwest is fighting this transfer of the National Energy Board to Alberta. It may be the transformation he made when he went in to a party without any western members. That could be, I do not know.
I would like my hon. friend from British Columbia to explain if he knows whether this is an organized plot to prevent the National Energy Board from going to Calgary.

Mr. Speaker, I tried to make it plain that I was speaking for the employees and asking for fair treatment for the employees.
I am going to read briefly from a letter from the Ontario Federation of Labour:
Government Orders
Giving people a choice of being out of work or of moving hundreds of miles away is really no choice at all. And to find out that this decision has been made by watching television has only added salt to the wounds of the employees.
We expect employers to treat their employees with dignity and respect. These workers were treated with what can only be seen as contempt and disdain.
We do expect the government to be a little better than the average employer when it comes to treating its employees fairly. We do not expect it to keep secrets like this when there is absolutely no reason that we know of, no reason has been advanced, for keeping it a secret until the last moment.
What I am talking about is fairness to the employees. I am not talking about the location in Calgary. I have lived a little while in Ottawa and during the war I lived a while in Calgary. There is not a heck of a lot by which to choose but if I had my choice I would go to Calgary. They do not have time to find that out before they have to make their decisions.

The minister asks why we are concerned.
We are concerned about people. That is why we are concerned. This government has not looked after the people who have made the National Energy Board what it is, which is a really good and responsible agency of the people of Canada. That is why we want to make sure their concerns are addressed.
I just heard another Tory member of Parliament discounting Manitoba entirely, talking about this caucus having no western members in it. Has he not heard about Manitoba? Has he not heard about B.C.? Are the prairies to him just Alberta and Saskatchewan?
I want to ask a question of the previous speaker. He seems remarkably uninformed about the situation of the employees. That is typical of NDP members. They tend to get up and speak at the last minute, try to get themselves a briefing with one person who is supposed to give them the truth from on high, and do not really know what is on the minds of the people they are talking about.
The hon. member seemed to imply that the schedule for this move is all right, even though it requires people to make a decision by next week to disrupt their whole lives, while the government has another full five months

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
actually to implement its decision. Does he think that is fair? Does he think it is fair that people who are relocating with the board are getting special and privileged treatment, and people who cannot, are not?

Mr. Speaker, it is not fair that any employee should be treated in that manner. That is the point I was trying to make in my speech, that we are concerned about fairness for the employees. We are concerned about it whether the Liberals or the Tories are in charge of the move. There have been examples of decentralization that the Liberals have implemented where they paid no more attention to the concerns of the employees than the Tories are today. They are both wrong. The employees should be the ones that are treated with real concern when their lives are being uprooted in the way that some of their lives are going to be uprooted in this case. It is wrong whether it is the Liberals or the Tories that do it.

Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in this debate on Bill C-2 simply to make a few comments on the fate of the National Energy Board's present employees who live in the National Capital Region, mostly in Ottawa, which I tiy to represent as best I can.
Mr. Speaker, the arguments for moving the National Energy Board may be valid and I suppose they are for some western MPs. I have heard some convincing arguments but I hear contrary ones from my constituents and I would like to put the remarks I am about to make in this context.
We must not forget the very important human factor involved. I remember that we had an interesting debate in this House in 1989 on Bill C-16, creating the Canadian Space Agency and dealing with other matters. Mr. Speaker, it will be remembered that the main concern then was for the public servants and workers affected by that decision.
Mr. Speaker, the number of positions at the National Energy Board has gone from 50 in 1959 when it was created to nearly 330 today, in 1991-92. The Public Service Commission report, which I have consulted, shows that the National Energy Board had 291 employees in 1990, of whom 273 were in the Ottawa area. This means that 273 families will have to choose in the next six months to relocate to another city in another
province or, if they decide not to move, hope to find other employment. The lives of 273 families will be put in turmoil by this government which I think has been insensitive by not foreseeing in its bill a situation that could be distressing for many of them. The proof, Mr. Speaker, is that I have letters from constituents who express quite eloquently the situation their families find themselves in, with children at school or university. They will have to make a serious decision: Do they move or do they break up the family, in a sense, leaving the children to complete their education here? Do they take the children with them, and God knows the problems that can mean socially and for their education.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, the testimony of one of my constituents shows veiy well how hard this decision is. This lady left her native province almost 20 years ago. She settled in the region, here in Ottawa, with her husband, who works for the National Energy Board. They have laid down roots here, Mr. Speaker. Their daughter attends the University of Ottawa; their son is in high school. The woman works. She has found a satisfying job that she loves and would like to keep and of which she is veiy proud. If her husband decides to leave Ottawa, they will have to decide what to do about the children.
If she chooses to follow her husband, Mr. Speaker, which is quite normal, the separation between the children and their parents will be painful. She will have to leave her job that she loves. There is no guarantee that she will find another one in Calgary. Once the school year is over or once they have completed high school or university, because it is not easy to move from one institution to another, the children will also have to decide on a career.
When you are 20 or 30, Mr. Speaker, those decisions can be made and it is sometimes exciting to relocate and have new experiences in another place in this great country of ours. For a family, it can be very trying at times. The responsibilities are great and I think that the choice can be a nightmare.
Mr. Speaker, of the 291 person-years or persons affected by this decision, 131 are in managerial, scientific, professional or technical positions. The NEB or National Energy Board estimates that 50 per cent of the employees will remain in Ottawa. That is an estimate. This means that the Board's expertise will be cut in half. Fifty per cent, or some 65 to 70 additional people, will
May 23, 1991

have to be hired to replace those who decide not to move.
Mr. Speaker, what will happen to those people who decide not to follow their employer to Calgary? They will be put on a priority list for one year. What will happen to them after a year? I do not know. Mr. Speaker, 80 of those 291 employees are French-speaking. Although Calgary is a friendly city, as I admit, and Alberta as a whole has a large, lively French-speaking community, our perception of Alberta is a province that is stingy in providing services to the linguistic minority. Therefore these French-speaking public servants, who make up 27.5 per cent of those who will have to relocate or leave their job, are legitimately concerned about their children's education and whether they will obtain in Alberta the same services that they had here in Ottawa, Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, the question is, can the government offer any hope to these public servants, these families who heard the news, as we all know, through the media. The news was announced the day before a budget. I wonder why these employees were treated differently from those who worked for the Space Agency?
To get back to that experience, I would like to remind hon. members that although the second reading stage of a bill is basically intended as an opportunity to consider the principle of the bill, and we acknowledged that principle, as I said earlier, because there are a number of pros- There are many reasons why we supported this initiative, but there is also reason to be worried about the human factor, about what will happen to the Canadian men and women who are now working at the National Energy Board.

I want to remind members of clauses in Bill C-16, an act to establish the Canadian Space Agency and to provide for other matters in relation to space.
Section 28(1) of that bill states:
Where a position in the Public Service of Canada is transferred to the Agency within ninety days after the day on which this Act comes into force, the incumbent of the position continues in the position in the Agency, unless the incumbent otherwise elects prior to the transfer, and any person so continuing is deemed to have been appointed to the Agency in accordance with subsection 16(1).
Government Orders
Then it goes on to subsection 2.
The preoccupation at that time was identified by Brian Leddy, the National Research Council's Vice President of Personnel. He said they were preoccupied with the anxiety about the problems of uprooting families, getting French language training and finding suitable schools for children.
Mr. Leddy said in an interview, and I quote from The Ottawa Citizen, March 19, 1990:
All the government's regular workforce adjustment programs,
including early retirement, severance packages and retraining would
be available to eligible individuals.
That experience is not, in my view, at least from what I understand and from what I have heard, going to be repeated with the transfer of the board to Calgary. I would think that in committee the government would want to answer some questions.
I give credit to previous speakers for raising this issue.
I agree with my colleague from Ottawa West on her comments. I know the member will be in committee, bringing forward some of the concerns people in the Ottawa area have expressed to us but not specifically about the move. As I have said, there are reasons to support it and there are also reasons against it. However, we are talking about the principle of second reading here.
If I know my rules, the principle of the bill is at stake here. That is the most important part, as far as I am concerned, of any bill's process, the principle being that the decision has been made by the government to move an agency to Calgary from its Ottawa head office location by law. All the bill does, essentially, is make it possible for the board and its employees to be outside the national capital, in Calgary. What happens after that? I guess the government will not have to come to Parliament any more if it wants to move the board to any other place in Canada.
Section 1 says very clearly that after the move to Calgary the Governor in Council may approve any decisions to relocate the board. I think that would also be of some concern to some people and we might want to get some explanation from the minister in committee.
But to come back to my point.

May 23, 1991
Government Orders

It is pretty obvious to a member who represents his constituents, and the hon. member for Ottawa West said as much as 70 per cent of our public servants are outside Ottawa and scarcely 20 per cent work in Ottawa. There may be 27 or 30 per cent in the National Capital Region as a whole, including the Quebec side, the Outaouais region.
In my own riding I have about 10 per cent, but for obvious reasons, I have a lot of these people living in Ottawa-Vanier who wrote letters expressing very strongly their reluctance, their worries and the problems they had.
As far as the principle is concerned, we acknowledge that the decision has been made and it is going to happen, but we now have to decide how it will be done, and that, I think, is what the legislative committee will have to consider. How will the government ensure that no employee's rights are violated, and that employees do not suffer economically, socially or in their family life?
Mr. Speaker, that is why the Liberal caucus, through its critic and the hon. member for Ottawa West and the hon. member for Carleton-Gloucester, did not express the kind of reservations the Solicitor General wanted to use to turn this into a partisan issue. We did not make this a partisan issue. We said that the decision was made, and we respect that decision. It was the government's decision. It wasn't our decision but the government's. As I said earlier, there are many reasons for thinking this could have been done differently, with more consultation, with a little more tact, with more attention to the personal and human factors. It was not done and we deplore that, but there are times when in this kind of situation, special measures must be taken after the fact.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, before expediting this bill through the House, I think it is only fair that the bill should go to committee, so that the minister has a chance to explain and we can have the assurance that this government, which in the case of the transfer of the Space Agency to Montreal was receptive to certain comments by Opposition members, that this government will also be receptive in this particular case and that it will deal sensitively with the employees who will be asked to move.
Is the House ready for the question?
Question.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion.
Agreed.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-8, an act to provide for the dissolution of the transfer of certain Crown corporations and to amend certain acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendment) from the legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada) moved
subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT

Motion agreed to.

subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: that the bill be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today for more than one reason.
I want to address the third reading of what was known as Bill C-73. This is an act that deals with the dissolution and reorganization of several Crown corporations.
One of the aspects of this that gives me some pleasure-and I hope it gives my colleagues some pleasure-is that we have an opportunity to resurrect or revive a bill that died at the end of the last session of the House.
In being able to do that, I think all of us in the House can manifest a degree of co-operation that for most purposes will enhance and further the interests of the taxpayer who pays for the cost of running this place. Also, it would advance the speed with which we deal with the bill and thereby permit government to get on with the work that is specifically proposed.
This particular bill has had the benefit of significant scrutiny at the legislative committee stage. That is one of
May 23, 1991

the reasons why we in opposition at this point in time are able to conclude that Parliament and the public have sufficiently examined what lies behind the bill and its purposes. This enables it to be dealt with reasonably expediently here in this new session.
I want to congratulate the chair of that legislative committee and the members on it for the way in which the bill was handled at committee. However, I want to raise an item of caution. It relates to the way the government has proposed legislative committees to deal with bills such as Bill C-73 in the future.
We all know that in the new rules that were passed here a few weeks ago, legislative committees are only permitted to call witnesses on technical matters. I objected to that restriction at the time the rule was passed, as did many others on this side of the House.
I would like to point out that if committees in the future follow that rule strictly, that is deal with technical matters only, then the very full review of Bill C-73 at legislative committee will not be able to take place in this House in the future. That is a negative in terms of procedure.
I want to caution Parliament about that and about a too rigid application of that restriction on legislative committees in the new rules. Committees must have sufficient latitude and not just deal with crossing the t's and dotting the i's on a bill, or whether the words put on paper will effectively accomplish the legal purpose of the bill.
We also have to give some attention to what the effect of the bill will be, based on the procedures that the bill proposes.
In this particular case dealing with the dissolution of these Crown corporations, all the members on the committee-not just the opposition, but the government members-did spend some time thinking about what would take place after the provisions of the bill were in place, giving authority to government officials to do certain things with Crown corporations.
There are six parts to this bill. There were two in particular that involved the disposition or sale of Crown assets of significant value. One involved B.C. Place in Vancouver where the federal government owns the land and the facility and the other involved Harbourfront Corporation in the city of Toronto. In both cases, the
Government Orders
government owns millions and millions of dollars worth of real estate.
In this particular bill the provision simply said that the minister, in most cases the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Transport as the case may be, would dispose of the government holding, as he or she thought appropriate. That is an awfully vague provision without much in the way of oversight by this Parliament.
That bill simply asked parliamentarians to say: "Yes, Minister of Public Works, you may take this asset worth $200 million, $300 million or $400 million and sell it as you think best". The taxpayers of Canada have an interest in how the government sells a $300 million or $400 million asset in bits and pieces. In committee we had to inquire into what the proposal was.
Regarding B.C. Place, and I want this to be on the record-it is on the committee record as well-the government has stated that it will dispose of it in a way that, at a minimum, gives the local governments in Vancouver the right to acquire it. I believe the intention is to actually move the asset over to provincial or municipal ownership.
We did not get the same assurances regarding Harbourfront in Toronto. I should also mention that in relation to other portions of Bill C-73 there were other assurances given by the government appearing before the committee as to what it would do when the assets were disposed of, when the corporations were dissolved.
In dealing with the Harbourfront Corporation, which is the one major corporation involving much more money than any of the others-a few hundred millions of dollars, mostly real estate assets-we in opposition had three concerns. We were reflecting concerns put forward, not just by our constituents, but by the government of the city of Toronto and the government of metropolitan Toronto. I do not believe that the provincial government itself has raised any caution flags, but I am sure we tried our best to accommodate their role in the disposition of this very significant harbour front asset.
All three areas were dealt with at committee. Believe me, they were more than just technical matters, much more than that. As a result of the committee inquiries and the communication that was had during and subsequent to the committee inquiries, a number of the misunderstandings or questions that existed then have been resolved. The real tough questions involved in Harbourfront have not been resolved. Those hard ques-

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
tions involve money. Unfortunately we do not always have a solution to money problems.
However, I would like to run through those areas for the benefit of the record. The first involved what appeared at the time to be a very significant premium being given to three large Canadian developers who were very active in the Toronto waterfront. At the time the Harbourfront transition committee, which was composed of Harbourfront officials and directors, had publicly recorded their projection that the premium, the giveaway that the developers would receive, would amount to approximately $36.6 million.
There is no one in this place who could sit here and not be disturbed at the prospect of the taxpayer doing a land swap or a flip with developers which gives them $36.6 million more than they give back to the taxpayer. That issue was raised and discussed. Subsequently, because of public concerns about this the city of Toronto commissioned a consultant study. That study was just recently published and made public.
It appears that the premium which was initially expressed to be approximately $36 million is estimated by this particular group of consultant to be in the vicinity of $5 million or $6 million. I do not want to say that now it is only $5 million or $6 million and that it is not a big deal so let us forget it; $6 million bucks is still $6 million bucks. In a fair, objective guess by a consultant, which is all they can do, that premium now, on the public record, is calculated to be closer to the $6 million level.
As one prominent individual who was quite involved in this process of resolving the Harbourfront challenges has pointed out, an expropriation process which the public, the federal government, the province, the city or metro could embark on, would cost as much as $5 million. By the time they have finished with new evaluations of the properties, retaining solicitors for all parties involved in the process, dealing with any expropriation hearings that might result in the event that there was a failure to agree and significant costs by the developers in preparing the lands for development there now based on existing
zonings or zonings they thought they might have, it could possibly cost $5 million.
At one point the city of Toronto and the province of Ontario were so concerned about this area that they actually, by ministerial order, froze development and rezoning activity on all of these lands. If you are a developer and owned these lands, as soon as the freeze went on someone has a hand in your pocket because you were stuck with an asset that was not producing income and it was frozen. I think we should recognize that as an economic reality.
Now that the premium is guessed to be $6 million, I leave that on the public record. If the government's view is that the premium is worth it, valid, viable and acceptable to the taxpayers, then that government will bear the responsibility for that deal when it takes place. There is nothing that we in opposition are going to be able to do to derail it once this bill goes through. The public will then make the decision.
The first issue, the swamp of the pipeline lands, we consider to have been adequately canvassed and developed on the public record, including the record of this House.
The second involved the endowment fund. This is easily canvassed. It is the money issue. The Harbourfront Corporation has carried on for years extremely valuable cultural, artistic, athletic and public participation programs on the Toronto waterfront. These were programs and activities in a city urban culture that simply would never be there if Harbourfront did not exist. That was the legacy of politicians and government officials from almost 20 years ago.
The concern of Torontonians was that this entity would be able to continue after the federal government completed its job of reshuffling ownership and basically getting out of the business of providing cultural entertainment on the Toronto Harbourfront. I take it that is the government's objective. I might object to that. I am of the view that the federal government is involved in providing cultural programming and support in a number of Canada's cities, Toronto included. I am of the view that it should continue.
May 23, 1991

In any event, the deficit issue, the endowment fund issue for Harbourfront, the federal government has stated that it will be in a position to pay into an endowment fund for Harbourfront $80 million from the sale of Harbourfront real estate assets. That is after the land swaps and all of the other rezonings and activities which must take place.
If they give $80 million, it is the view of most who look at the scene that the income from that endowment fund would be insufficient to maintain Harbourfront even at its current reduced level of activity. I accept that there are those who call many federal institutions fat cows-no disrespect to cows-and that perhaps we should all be trying to make federal institutions get along with a bit less money. I am going to use the calculations that were provided in the report produced only two or three days ago and made public at City of Toronto Council. They are as follows.
If the $80 million fund is used in perpetuity to provide income only to Harbourfront, that $80 million will finance a funding shortfall, a revenue shortfall, at Harbourfront of only $1.5 to $3.5 million per year. I will not make any value judgment on whether or not that is a lot of income. I simply put that on the record.
If the $80 million is simply viewed as a fund from which Harbourfront will draw income and capital to finance deficits over the foreseeable future, Harbourfront's funding from that endowment fund will only last according to the consultants until 2003.
The third possibility had to do with an if. If the federal government-or all levels of government-were able to commit to fund Harbourfront at a level that was consistent both with its past level of expenditure and revenue and its projected level of expenditure and revenue, and based on the shrinkage factor that I have just alluded to, the endowment fund according to the consultant would have to be at least $193 million, roughly double what the government is proposing to provide now.
I will leave those facts and figures there. It is our view here on this side of the House that our role now is to point out these things. The harder decisions will be in the hands of the Minister of Public Works as he or she disposes of assets and takes the money and puts it into an endowment fund.
Harbourfront is going to live and thrive or it is not, or maybe we will stumble along somewhere in the middle. My view is that Harbourfront should live and thrive and continue to do the work it has always done on the Toronto Harbourfront.
Before moving out of the debate here, I wanted to raise another caution flag. It is important when pursuing the public discussion and the communication that have permitted us to deal with this publicly that we deal with the concept of commercial confidentiality. Even today, as I stand here now, I am unable to obtain information that would permit me to make an even better judgment about this.
Regarding the commercial confidentiality imposed or requested by the developers or by the public individuals who have been working on this issue, I understand where it comes from. It is a request by individuals that evaluations of their corporate assets, their strategic goals and their development proposals not be made public. The problem I have with that is that we are dealing with public assets here. We are already dealing with what the taxpayers own. I start off looking at this whole area and saying we cannot permit confidentiality to preclude the taxpayer from knowing everything that is going on with these assets.
I see, Mr. Speaker, you wish to take note of the clock.

subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
It now being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair until two o'clock this day.
The House took recess at 1 p.m.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, on February 11 of this year, the Minister of Finance tried to pull a fast one on Canadians. On that day, he issued what appeared to be a harmless press release concerning some technical matters dealing with family and private trusts. What it

May 23, 1991
really amounted to was perhaps the biggest tax windfall for the wealthy in history.
In 1972, a law was passed which stipulated that after 21 years any increase in the value of assets in trusts would be subject to a capital gains tax. That meant that in 1993 the government would have come into billions of dollars in tax revenue. Instead, what was proposed was a loophole that allows the tax to be put off for decades.
Isn't that something? While the national debt is being saddled on the backs of the working and middle class, the wealthy get the tax breaks.
Why were these changes not announced in the budget that was delivered only days later? Why was no estimate of lost revenue provided to the Canadian people? Indeed, this would have proved too embarrassing for the government.
After all, it was the Minister of Finance who said: "I am asking Canadians to share the burden of fiscal restraint-the challenge to all Canadians is to do what each of us can do to strengthen our country."
It seems that this government wants to challenge some Canadians more than others. Of course, the fight against the deficit will go on.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian ambassador to the UN announced yesterday, at the first session of the United Nations Economic and Social Council, that the Canadian Parliament will ratify by the end of the year the bill of rights approved at the Summit for Children held in New York City two years ago.
In September 1989, prime minister Mulroney was co-chairman of the international conference. By January 1991, Canada had already set up a children's bureau coming under health and welfare Canada. Benoit Bouchard is the minister in charge of coordinating all government programs to ensure they are in keeping with the provisions of the bill of rights. Canada also invested $136 million this past February to support the fight against family violence.
Mr. Speaker, these are concrete steps taken by this government to help families tom by family violence.

Mr. Speaker, in his frenzy to cut costs, the Minister of Transport is permitting security firms to undercut one another as they scramble to secure contracts with airports. They do this without any regard for existing wage rates or respect for existing collective agreements.
At Terminal 1, the security firm Aeroguard is demanding a wage cut of $2 an hour from its employees as well as elimination of a group insurance plan. The company is threatening the 100 passenger screening agents with lay-offs if they refuse these cuts designed to get the contract for Aeroguard.
How long is this government and the Ministers of Transport and Labour going to allow these conditions to persist? When are workers rights going to be protected? When is this government going to realize that the safety of the travelling public depends on skilled workers? When is this government going to live up to the words of a previous transport minister who stated that he would not permit such contracts to be let on the backs of workers?

Mr. Speaker, a recently completed United Nations survey confirmed what many of us in this country have known for a long time, that Canada is a great place to live.
Through examination, a number of categories including health standards, education, social conditions, taxation system and disposable income, the UN determined Canada ranks second only to Japan in terms of over-all standard of living.
It seems incredible to me that there are those in this country who are willing to risk all that we have attained as a country over the past 125 years to pursue their own narrow political aims.
It is time we, as Canadians, started to work together to ensure we remain the envy of the rest of the world.
May 23, 1991

Mr. Speaker, today I rise to bring to the attention of the House the victory of the Prince Edward Island Armour Fence Hockey Team in the Canadian Allan Cup Triple "A" Hockey Championships.
The Islanders dramatic 5 to 4 win over the Thunder Bay Twins 57 seconds into overtime brought the best of seven finals to a close in a four game sweep at the Charlottetown Civic Centre. This win has earned Prince Edward Island its first ever Allan Cup victory.
It is very admirable when provinces with such a small population as that of Prince Edward Island produces such a victorious team. Indeed, this is an occasion when the other provinces can take note and look with admiration towards the maritimes.
On behalf of all Islanders, I wish to congratulate the Armour Fence Islanders on their impressive championship win and express our most heartfelt pride in the example they have set through their tenacity, enthusiasm and outstanding sportsman-like conduct.
Congratulations team. You've earned the recognition and pride of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow is Sneaker Day, marking once again the kick-off of Canada's Fitweek.
Throughout the week and until June 2, a number of events are planned to promote healthy active living.
To highlight in a special way the first day of this week featuring physical activity, all Canadians including members of this House are invited to wear their sneakers tomorrow.
Canada's Fitweek is the largest celebration of physical activity in the world, Mr. Speaker, as no less than eight million people across the country will participate in over
14,000	events already scheduled.
Canada's Fitweek now has an enviable world-wide reputation that all Canadians have every reason to be proud of.
In closing, I would like to point out that the success of this celebration is due, to a large extent, to the 300,000 volunteers who have organized the various activities in most cities in the country. I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to thank them for their dedication.

Mr. Speaker, last year the people of Slovenia, Croatia and Macedonia experienced democracy for the first time in half a century.
More recently, Croatians and Slovenians, by way of referendum, have expressed their willingness to withdraw from the chaos that is Yugoslavia today.
The republics and provinces of Yugoslavia have failed to agree on a leader, and the collective presidency is mired in discord. The evolving democracy is now in danger of being ambushed by military rule and occupation.
I call upon the government to respect the democratic wishes of the people who live in Slovenia, Croatia and Macedonia and to be prepared to recognize whatever form of government they choose.

Mr. Speaker, after Switzerland and the United States, Canada is the oldest federal system in the world.
Great nations are not built on a foundation of common language or common territorial boundaries, but rather by people who have done great things together in the past and who intend to do great things together in the future.
In the past, working together, Canadians have explored and settled half a continent, created a nation from the Atlantic to the Pacific to the Arctic Oceans; built a transcontinental transportation and communications system and developed the seventh strongest economy, the second highest standard of living and a social safety network which is the envy of the world.

May 23, 1991
If we are to stay united in the future, Canadians need a new national agenda to work for, an agenda which includes a clean environment, a just resolution of aboriginal concerns and the elimination of illiteracy, hunger, homelessness and violence.
But whatever our new national agenda may be, it should certainly be more than just a desire to repeal the Official Languages Act.

Mr. Speaker, the UN has just released its 1991 Human Development Report. This report shows that the gap between rich and poor countries continues to grow.
What is the Mulroney government doing about this deteriorating global situation? It is reneging on Canada's long held commitment to international development.
In the past three years alone, the government has cut billions of dollars from our international development funding commitments.
CIDA, along with hundreds of development NGOs and hundreds of thousands of Canadian volunteers, through their very hard work over the years, have given Canada a solid reputation as a world leader in the field of development assistance. Now this government wants to dismantle CIDA and undermine the work of our development NGOs.
The government should be working with development NGOs to increase the amount of Canadian aid going to those people who need it most and who need it urgently.

Mr. Speaker, as a result of my Point of Order yesterday, several comments were made in the House that private members on the government side should be restricted from asking questions.
In fact, we represent more Canadians than any other group in the House and in many cases Question Period is the only tool we have to get the attention to issues affecting our constituents. Often we will disagree with the position of the government or a minister, or a
minister may not understand the urgency of a problem in a region like Atlantic Canada. Question Period is the most effective place to get our point across.
On the other hand, government members should not use Question Period for planted questions, and oppositions should stop using it for speech-making and grandstanding.
If we all are a little more responsible, we can have a lot more questions and a whole lot more answers. Instead of trying to gain points for our own benefit, maybe we should try to do more for the people who sent us here.

Mr. Speaker, I bring to the attention of this House a serious problem both within my constituency, the federal constituency of St. Boniface, and throughout Canada; the teaching of English or French as a second language to new Canadians.
This is particularly important in view of the increased number of immigrants because of this government's decision.
In early March, 1991 I received a petition from over 225 constituents, mostly volunteers who were working with these people to help them learn the language and to integrate into society. They requested support for language instruction.

Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand petitions signed by more than 225 constituents asking me to:
-support their request that courses in English as a second
language be given in St. Boniface for adult refugees who do not
speak English, upon their arrival.

My constituents want these new Canadians to learn English now so they can integrate fully into Canadian society, find jobs and become active participants as soon as possible.
I wrote to the appropriate minister on March 11 and again on April 12. Why have my constituents not received an answer?
May 23, 1991



Are they not important enough? Surely the question requires an immediate answer.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow, May 24 is Sneaker Day, the day when all Canadians, including members of the House, are invited and encouraged to wear their sneakers in support of healthy, active living.
Sneaker Day is the kick-off event for Canada's Fit-week, running from tomorrow until June 2. This country can take great pride in knowing that Canada's Fitweek is now recognized internationally as the largest celebration of physical activity in the world.
This year, more than eight million Canadians are expected to participate in over 14,000 events taking place across Canada. Canada's Fitweek is co-ordinated by the Government of Canada through fitness and amateur sport, the provincial and territorial governments and 16 national organizations. At the community level, hundreds of thousands of volunteers contribute their time and energy to this annual celebration. The growth of Fitweek can only be described as phenomenal.
Canada's Fitweek is an excellent example of government and the corporate sector working together to promote the message of active living to Canadians and to maintain the momentum of the fitness movement.
During the next 10 days, I invite all members to join Canadians from coast to coast in promoting and participating in the many events planned in their own constituencies as part of Canada's Fit Week.

Mr. Speaker, is the Solicitor General aware that video games, which puts the player in the role of concentration camp manager and which dehumanizes Jews and Turks, have been available in Germany and Austria for over a year. According to some news reports, it is possible that
these racist video games, which amount to hate propaganda, originate in Canada.
Does the minister intend to investigate the possibility that these games originate here and take action to limit their distribution.

The German police has said that the demand for, and availability of, these racist games has increased over the past year. Does the minister intend to take action to ensure that these games are not distributed in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation is completing its thirtieth year of service. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disease affecting the lungs and digestive system of children and young adults.
Following the very recent discovery of the gene that causes cystic fibrosis, the Foundation is asking for everyone's help more than ever. Their theme this year, their thirtieth anniversary, is: "Thirty years of caring-Proof of the power of dreams".
I wish to thank the Foundation, the thousands of volunteers working with it and those who contributed the $6 million collected this year for research, services and public education. Congratulations and best wishes for success to the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation.

Mr. Speaker, a survey on personal safety in Ottawa was published today. While the results may be a surprise to some, for women it was a frightening reality. One-third of women feel unsafe in their own neighbourhoods. Almost 90 per cent of women feel they must limit their own activities. They believe they are at greater risk simply because they are female. I am not surprised by these statistics for they do reflect the views of the lives of women across Canada.
Women are also at risk in their own homes. The assaults and murders of women by their partners shows this reality. Because that danger is also outside the home, women have developed methods of coping with

Oral Questions
this danger and fear. We walk home only in well-lit areas. We park our cars near the few lights in parking lots. We stay out of parks at night. We try to ignore the rude comments of strangers.
We need more than a blue ribbon panel on violence against women. We need programs and action. We need action from this government now to end violence against women.

Mr. Speaker, I was horrified to learn recently that a wonderful and committed participant from Guatemala to the United Nations Conference in Geneva, Mr. Miguel Sucuqui, has had to go into hiding because of his work there.
On May 6, 1991, a government backed paramilitary group came to his home to arrest him. When they could not find him, they threatened the lives of his wife and family.
This is not the only incident of violence by Guatemalan authorities against participants at the Geneva meeting. Mr. Camilo Ajqui Jimon was assassinated on April 14. At least one other has suffered an attempted kidnapping.
There are others who are now living in mortal fear because of their work at the United Nations and for human rights generally.
Today, I am writing to the Guatemalan government to express my concern regarding these particular incidents. I call upon the government to do the same immediately.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The verdict on the GST is in. In the first three months, Canadian retailers have suffered the worst sales record since the history of record keeping. We find again today that sales are down. In Kingston alone in a survey by a national
accounting firm, Ernst and Young, one in two Kingston families do their shopping south of the border.
Canadians are voting with their feet and they are voting by shopping south of the border. In that survey, Ernst and Young predicted that 500 jobs would be lost in Kingston alone as a result of that particular problem.

Mr. Speaker, on the point just made by my colleague from Scarborough- Rouge River, it is important to put on record the fact that what is happening here on Toronto's waterfront is a wholesale withdrawal of responsibility on the part of the federal government. This involves not only Toronto but other cities of Canada where there is a federal presence in the form of publicly owned lands.
What we see here today is the continuation of a Tory agenda whereby there is retreat from government. There is a belief that the public interest is better served by not providing certain services and by abandoning, in the case of Harbourfront, a very important investment made on behalf of the Canadian people 20 years ago in favour of some kind of sale of land, the outcome of which is still uncertain.
I refer to the plan whereby an endowment would be set up by way of the sale of Crown owned assets at Harbourfront. We do not know what the revenue will be from the sale. I can tell you that this fact alone casts a very large shadow on the credibility of the measure being proposed in this bill by the government.
We are told that what is required is an endowment of roughly $193 million that would permit the continuation of public programs, a variety of activities that take place at Harbourfront in Toronto. This city is represented by many colleagues of mine on this side of the House. The $193 million amount is not at all secure in the estimates being carried out by the city and metro. We understand the amount of the endowment that can be calculated at this stage and relied upon is roughly $80 million. In other words, what is required is 2.5 times the amount that seems to be predictable as the size of the endowment itself. Instead of $193 million, we are told we can count on an endowment resulting from the sale of these lands of some $80 million, which will result in a yearly deficit after revenue of some $8 million to $9 million.
It does not take a great accountant to realize what is happening here. Considerable cuts will have to be made
to public programs which so far Torontonians have enjoyed year after year on their waterfront, at Harbourfront. The Tory government has decided they should be considerably reduced.
What is happening here in essence is that the federal government is threatening to walk away from Harbourfront. It is proposing with this bill an initiative that will leave the Harbourfront administration or its successor in a situation whereby it will not be able to support the present activities. The public will therefore suffer the consequences.
I cannot understand for the life of me why the minister in charge of this bill did not take the trouble today to put before us in the opposition and the public, through the media, the exact situation that has evolved over time. In other words, we are debating in a cloud of uncertainty. We do not know what are the exact figures. We can only make certain conclusions based on assumptions made by the city of Toronto property department and in a study that was prepared for metro some time ago.
I ask whether this is the way to run a government. Is this the way to manage the public interest? Is this the way to plan future recreational activities of a population of some 3.5 million people in the metro area? People of all ages and backgrounds of the entire metro region flock to Harbourfront on weekends in particular and during the week in order to enjoy the variety of programs.
This is politically an irresponsible way to proceed. I submit that this government is proceeding in a manner that will be remembered by the voters at the next election. Unless our assumptions are completely wrong-and this is why I am objecting strenuously to the fact that the minister did not take the trouble to put forward and define the situation-this will result, in the very near future, in a reduction of existing program activities and recreation at Harbourfront.
We have on this side of the House systematically said that these lands ought not to be sold, that these lands were bought for the public, and that they should remain in public ownership. They represent the only real estate or property that allows the citizens of metro Toronto direct access to their greatest and best ecological asset, namely their lake. As a result of this bill, this is no longer going to be the case for certain lands at Harbourfront.

We have here two losses. The first is the loss on the investment made. As I said, it was the result of a decision made in 1972 by a forward looking government. The second is the loss of a variety of culturally rich and much appreciated recreational programs on the waterfront which have attracted tens of thousands of people.
I have submitted these thoughts, Mr. Speaker, for your consideration in the hope that finally someone on behalf of the government will rise today and give a clear explanation of what exactly is going to be the situation in the city of Toronto and metro Toronto regarding the disposition of these lands, particularly in relation to the future of the programs at Harbourfront.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have a few moments to speak on Bill C-8. I want particularly to address my remarks to four short sections, namely sections 40 through 44, because they deal with Harbourfront, which is in the municipality of metropolitan Toronto.
I represent the riding of Scarborough West and there are many in Scarborough West, as there are many throughout the municipality of metropolitan Toronto, who take great pleasure particularly on a Sunday afternoon to go down to Harbourfront and enjoy the many activities available. These are family times. People can take their families there and have a wonderful time.
In addition, tourists go there by the thousands and this has been nothing but a benefit to the community of metropolitan Toronto.
How might that be affected by this bill? I think it could very well be and the answer is simple: the bill is almost naked insofar as its provisions to the Harbourfront Corporation are concerned.
In section 40 the bill authorizes the Minister of Public Works to procure the dissolution of Harbourfront Corporation, period. No guidance; simply go ahead and dissolve Harbourfront Corporation. One looks a little bit further to see what kind of guidance there should be and what sorts of criteria there should be; should there be a bottom-line sale price, whatever. The next section talks about the minister directing the corporation "to sell or otherwise dispose of any or all of its assets".
No direction whatsoever. No indication at all of what the corporation should be doing or how the corporation should be dissolving its assets.

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
We look further. We continue to look for guidance. We look to subsection 3 of section 41. The Minister of Public Works is authorized to do what with the money from the sale? I quote:
-to pay all or any part of the proceeds of any disposition of its assets-to such person and on such terms and conditions as are approved by the Governor in Council.
Who is the Governor in Council? It certainly is not the people of Canada, it is not the people of metropolitan Toronto. It is, in effect, the cabinet. The cabinet can make whatever decision it wants. There is no guidance in the legislation as to what that decision should be, could be or might be. No guidance whatsoever. There is guidance for the directors of Harbourfront Corporation because they are told that once receiving a direction from the minister, they are authorized to sell or dispose of the assets in accordance with the direction without any personal liability to the directors whatsoever.
Why might that be a problem? For one thing, let us talk about the people of the city of Toronto, the people of the municipality of metropolitan Toronto. We know that this issue has been considered by the municipality in its metropolitan council. We also know that metropolitan council believes that the lands which are currently in public ownership should not be sold for development.
One might wonder why. What is wrong with that? They address that issue and they indicate in their conclusion on page 5, which they have drawn to the attention of this government: "That the waterfront, in general, and Harbourfront specifically, is a regional resource, attracting not only residents of all six area municipalities, but residents from throughout the greater Toronto area, as well as a significant tourist population. It is therefore critical that the metropolitan interests in enhancing access to and along the waterfront be addressed".
Is there anything at all in Bill C-8 that addresses those issues? The answer is no. I have read sections 40 and 42. The other three sections are in effect legislative housekeeping. That is all. There is no guidance whatsoever.
We do know that the government has what I will call good intentions about an endowment fund, about the opportunity to protect this area for the citizens of metro Toronto and the surrounding region. What in heaven's name does that mean? What are good intentions? We have heard the phrase "the road to hell is paved with
good intentions". Good intentions without legislation are meaningless. The phrase used to be "good intentions and 25 cents will buy you a cup of coffee". I guess today you could say "good intentions and 75 cents will buy you a cup of coffee". Good intentions are still worth nothing.
It must be in the legislation and it is not in the legislation. If it is not in the legislation, there is no guarantee that the people of metropolitan Toronto will have that area protected for them.
What is the future to be? We have absolutely no idea what the future is going to be. Citizens of metropolitan Toronto are left to wonder, as everyone in this House is left to wonder, as to precisely what is going to occur when this government in effect privatizes Harbourfront and gets out of the business. This is after years and years of investing the taxpayers' money to build up Harbourfront. The taxpayers have put money into it. Now it is going to be dissolved. Are we going to get any money? We do not know. It depends on the real estate prices. Are the developers going to benefit? We do not know, but it looks like it.
We certainly do not know what the people of metropolitan Toronto are going to get out of it which will be beneficial. At this point I see nothing and guarantees of nothing.
I have to oppose Bill C-8 because of the lack of provisions dealing with Harbourfront.

subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to get on the record some concerns that I have about the process that is before us in the form of Bill C-8. It is difficult for the public to follow all of this.
This afternoon we are debating a federal bill which has to do with the disposition of lands in metropolitan Toronto. That sounds like a fairly straightforward piece of business. The truth is that it is not. Those of us who have followed this for some time know that Harbourfront has been the subject of a number of inquiries by four or five different levels of government.
This has gone on in a strange way. Most of us in this Chamber would advocate that the public's business ought to be transacted in public; that is, that the public has a right to see how the transaction is put together, who benefits and what the consequences of that are. This process has gone on for some time.

I recall when Harbourfront was first proposed the first things that went up were the billboards announcing Harbourfront. This went through I think about three or four federal elections. I could never find Harbourfront, only the billboards were there. Then eventually there was a place that one could identify as Harbourfront. As it grew it became a very vibrant part of the metropolitan Toronto and I dare say many people would argue that it is an international attraction at this time, that there are people from all over the world who are attracted to the Harbourfront in Toronto and to all of the activities that go on around that space.
It does seem strange then that this successful operation is now being marketed rather on the sly. There are different levels of government, including the province of Ontario, the city of Toronto, metropolitan Toronto and the federal government negotiating the disposition of these lands and the subsequent settlements about who will continue to run the programming on those lands.
I for one would argue that this is fine if that is what governments want to do, but at the very least the public has a right to know. All of us who sat on municipal councils, for example, would know that we would be in deep trouble at this stage if we tried to take an asset of any municipality in Canada, sell it off behind closed doors and do some kind of a deal that might continue the operation. Anybody who is on a council can try that tonight. Go home and tell your people you want to sell off the rink and do not worry about the operation of the arena in future years, we will work out some deal on the side. The rest of the council would have your scalp, and it ought to. That is not the way that the public's business ought to be dealt with.
The concerns I have centre around the way that the process has evolved. It is not that I have anything against David Crombie or Darcy McKeough, two very fine people who have worked very hard to try to put together something. There are a number of civil servants who have tried to deal with the problem of Harbourfront and how to go through a transitional period.
My concerns are pretty straightforward. At this point I do not know what will happen with those lands. I do know that the city, Metro, and the province of Ontario have all encountered great difficulty with developing plans for Harbourfront. They have had great difficulty
Government Orders
dealing with the development around there now. If you wanted to see the Harbourfront parklands in Toronto you really have to get a boat and and see it from the lake. You cannot see it from the city of Toronto. You can get there. You can walk along there but you certainly would never know that it is there from most of downtown Toronto.
It is liked by the people, it is actually a success and has become kind of a focal point for a great many cultural festivals and for artists who work there. A great many ordinary people go there on a Sunday afternoon and wander around. It is clearly something that the people like and want. It is generally acknowledged as being a good thing. Now, behind closed doors, a deal is being put together to get rid of these assets.
I think you need to know a little history of Harbourfront to understand that this is a place where parkland appears suddenly in the water; one of the few modem miracles. It is true that developers who dedicate parkland as part of a development project have found a new technique for creating parkland. They dump fill into the lake and that is proposed parkland agreed upon by three or four different levels of government. That is a strange phenomenon.
Now we are supposed to take this bill and say that we acknowledge that the development of the Harbourfront project in metro Toronto did not go exactly as people thought it would. The concept originally was to set all of the development back from the waterfront so that the public would continue to have access to the water and the parkland that were there. Subsequently there might be some high-rise development around it but it surely would not be set in place to block the view from the city of Toronto. That is what happened. We regret that.
I hope this will not be taken as a model. I am aware, as I am sure all members are, that all across the north shore of Lake Ontario there are harbours that used to be industrial harbours and are now controlled by federal agencies called harbour commissions. There is ongoing warfare in each and every one of those communities because the shipping industry is not what it used to be. Others are moving in and saying they would like to build some nice high-rise apartments on the harbour and sell them off as harbourfront property, just like in Ibronto. It is precisely this scheme that is being looked at all across the north shore of Lake Ontario from Hamilton in my area right out to the town of Newcastle. That includes

May 23, 1991
Government Orders
projects already in the books, with plans proposed for places like Oshawa, Whitby, and Ajax.
The development industry is aware that this government is setting a pattern with this bill. I am concerned about that pattern. I would be much happier if we could follow the transactions which are taking place behind closed doors. I have a concern that the first phase of this project might look not too bad. It would not be hard for me to imagine that the Government of Canada would put together a deal with several private sector developers who provided a lot of money up front for the property.
The expectation is clear that the programming, the cultural activities, the access to the waterfront, and the use of the waterfront park will continue. It will not be interrupted. What is not clear is how that is going to be funded. Will the Government of Canada simply say as it has on a couple of other occasions: "Well, that's nice. We concluded our business. Somebody else pick it up and run with it from here"? I am sure that the city of Toronto is not quite prepared to accept this kind of international facility as being solely its responsibility, nor is metro, nor is the province of Ontario. I think the ongoing business dealings and the working out of details become more and more important as this bill nears the final stages. I think that part is important.
I want to sound, not a clarion call, but I want to sound a warning of danger here, as I see this as a model for harbourfront property all across Canada now in the possession of the federal government, if this process works at this one site in metropolitan Toronto. This is a government that has at least set its course fairly clearly. It loves to privatize things. The federal Government of Canada owns a lot of waterfront property all across this nation, at one time used veiy actively for harbour purposes, for ship-building purposes, but now not quite so active.
My concerns are very clear. If this turns out to be the way we do things in the future, if waterfront property owned by the federal government across Canada is dealt with in this way-that is to say a bill of this nature which says simply: "we want to privatize things, sell off some land", and then backroom deals on how the land is
developed and how programming continues and what happens afterwards, and the rest is just left up in the air, if those deals are all private deals, struck with various civil servants or ministers of the Crown on what might happen, then I believe that the public has been gypped in this process.
The public initially paid a pretty hefty price for these lands. I think the public, as the property owners, have a right to know what the consequences of this bill and the subsequent transactions that are not a part of the bill will be, and what will happen in the future. They do not know that.
Any individual property owner who entered into this kind of negotiation would want to know all of the side bars. They would want to get their lawyers out and examine the fine print about what happens after the sale is concluded. People know that is important. The expectations of the public in Toronto, in metropolitan Toronto, in the province of Ontario, and indeed the taxpayers of Canada, who by and large funded this project initially, are to get something reasonable out of the sale.
Now there is no way for them to judge, because those negotiations are not a matter of public record yet, and probably will not be even after all the deals are concluded.
Those are my concerns. The initial problem of dealing with Harbourfront is hardly resolved by simply selling off the property. I do not think anybody would really advocate that.
However, there is a concern I have with the nature of going about that. Is it reasonable to say that all of the negotiations will be done virtually privately? That is quite wrong, it is a wrong way for a government to proceed. It is virtually immoral for any government to come forward with a bill of this nature which says, in very stark terms: "We want to privatize this particular harbourfront project", without full details accompanying it to explain to all of us just precisely how this thing is supposed to continue to operate. Is it the government's intent to turn it over to the private sector, lock, stock and barrel? That is, the physical assets of Harbourfront are sold now and somebody in the private sector is then supposed to arrange all of the cultural and artistic activities that will follow in years to come?

May 23, 1991

I understand that a developer would be very attracted to the notion of getting his or her hot little hands on this kind of prime waterfront property in downtown Toronto and operate some kind of programming on the side for a couple of years. I fail to see why they would have an interest in operating that for the next 20, 30, 40 or 50 years. The hard fact is that those developers, whatever their intentions might be today, are highly unlikely to be around and active in that project in 10 years. They will be long gone.
The nature of the development industry is to buy into a project like this, get something on the ground, get it sold, and get out of there. They do not see it as their responsibility-and I don't either-to run long-term cultural activities for metropolitan Toronto. I do not know of any developers around who have said: "It is our job as the private sector to run cultural activities for the next hundred years". I have never heard them say it and I doubt they would. I am sure many of them would say: "Well, if part of the condition of sale is that we do something for five years, we will be happy to do that because we can see where the end of that is".
I have many concerns about the specifics of this bill. I want to reiterate in closing my concerns about the pattern that is being set by this bill.
If this is the model that is to be used around Canada for disposing of waterfront property, this is the wrong model. I hope that it is not the model and that before this bill is concluded and dealt with by this House the minister would reply and give us the details of all the arrangements, all the little side bar agreements, concerning the continuing activities of Harbourfront.
I must admit that I know of a number of negotiations that are ongoing and of a number of people who have an interest. I do not know of any published accounts of the specifics of how it all will be handled, and I believe that to be crucial.

enriched immeasurably our cultural life in Toronto through operations such as the artists' galleries, the theatres, the dance theatre, and events like the International Author's Festival, which has Harbourfront as its home and has put Canada on the map around the world as being a cultural centre, a country which nourishes its authors.
When we take the step of privatizing this land we must be assured that the public trust is looked after, that for the years to come the harbourfront will be a place for people, a place for enjoyment, a place for culture, not just a place for development. We have lots of places for development in this country. Does it have to be the choicest land in Toronto? Can we assure that, in perpetuity, the land will be devoted to these purposes? This is my question to the hon. member.
What assurance, with this bill before us, do we have that the activities commenced in such laudable fashion by Harbourfront will continue, that the people of Toronto and the people of Canada will continue to benefit in perpetuity the way they have in the past?

Mr. Speaker, that is precisely the nature of my concern. There is absolutely no guarantee from anyone on record that I could find ensuring that those kinds of activities will continue for anything but a very short period of time. That is my concern. Even if I agreed that it was the proper route to go, then at least the Government of Canada has an obligation to conduct its public business publicly. That is not happening. By the time all of this is concluded, it may be literally impossible for anyone to do anything about it. That is wrong.
