speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member is accusing me of criticizing Bob Rae, he is only about five years too late. I suppose that is consistent with him. If he is accusing me of saying that the Government of Ontario should not be the prime mover in all this, he is right. Unfortunately it is not. It is not setting the pattern for how this is handled. This is essentially being done by the federal government.
If he is accusing members of the province of Ontario of being supreme controllers of how this kind of land is developed in Ontario, he is wrong because they are not. I bet at this moment they wish they were.
I wish that the powers of the provincial government superseded the powers of the federal government. If that were the case then we could certainly put a stop to this. If we could get agreement here this afternoon to make that the case, if everybody in the House was quite happy to say "listen, the feds have botched this one up too; let us turn this over to the province of Ontario", I think we might actually get it all straightened out.
I would certainly use all the pitiful amount of influence I have with anybody to see that this process gets opened up just a bit more.
Just to conclude, one of the problems with this Harbourfront project and its history over the last little while is that no one level of government has clear
responsibility over anything. I had a conversation with David Crombie, for example, on this matter. One of the things that he discovered is that there are some 50-odd agencies of different levels of government which have some measure of control over what happens in the Toronto harbour. That has been a major problem for eveiybody, because any time anyone wants to take some initiative, good or bad, the best that one can hope for is a stalemate, and that is wrong.
If the member wants to turn this over to the province of Ontario, I would be happy to do it. I am not sure the government would be prepared to do so, but, to tell you the truth, it would be a real good move on its part.

subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my friend makes a point about the different levels of government and different agencies having jurisdiction. We know now that the federal government owns land at Habourfront. We know as well that the province of Ontario has jurisdiction over planning, which is delegated to municipalities, in this case the city of Toronto.
The federal government has control because it does not have to sell the land. The provincial government can simply say: "Pursuant to the authority that we have vis-a-vis development and land use at this particular site, we are not going to allow any more development". Bob Rae does have the opportunity here. I accept my friend's point that he has been in some disagreement with the premier for some time. His criticism is well taken.
With regard to the federal government, it would be my view that this bill should not proceed, that we ought not to privatize Harbourfront. This entity provides the cultural activities which include an art gallery, the dance theatre, a children's summer camp, outdoor festivals, book readings and park and waterfront activities. We should not be privatizing Harbourfront. As well, the federal government should not be selling land to private interest, especially when that land happens to be parkland and when that land happens to be at the waterfront in metropolitan Toronto.
We know that the politicians and the bureaucrats have really goofed when it comes to metropolitan Toronto. I do not know when you last visited Toronto, Mr. Speaker, but you know that a number of very ugly buildings have been built over the last number of years at the water's edge in metropolitan Toronto. I do not know how the provincial government, the municipal government or the federal government allowed that to happen. The fact

that it has happened leads us to question very seriously what is going on with this particular bill.
My friend raised the concern about private dealings behind closed doors. There is a lot of private dealing going on and this government should put a stop to it.
This bill does not clearly indicate what is to happen. It simply gives authority under section 40 to the minister:
40.	(1) The Minister of Public Works is hereby authorized to procure, on behalf of Her Majesty in right of Canada, the dissolution of Harbourfront Corporation.
(2) The Minister of Public Works may do all things and perform all acts necessary for or incidental to closing out the affairs of Harbourfront Corporation.
And section 41:
41.	(1) Before Harbourfront Corporation is dissolved pursuant to section 40, the Minister of Public Works may direct the Corporation to sell or otherwise dispose of any or all of its assets, including shares of any other corporation-
One of the main assets that Harbourfront has is land. What is proposed-I cannot understand it for the life of me-is that public land owned by the Government of Canada is to be sold to private interests to put up expensive, luxury condominiums so developers can make a lot of money and so that rich people can have a coined with a balcony looking out over the beautiful water of Lake Ontario.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology

speechtext: What is wrong with that?

speechtext:
The Conservative member opposite says there is nothing wrong with the federal government selling public parkland in order to benefit the rich and wealthy.
There are a lot of poor people and not so poor people in metropolitan Toronto who cannot escape to Roscoe Lake on the hot summer weekends in order to boat at their cottages.
A lot of residents of metropolitan Toronto have the waterfront for their recreation during the summer months.
This government is proposing to sell that very valuable asset. Why? Not to reduce the deficit. We know that the government has gone to extremes in order to reduce the
Government Orders
national deficit, but it says it wants to sell part of the land in order to create a trust fund so that Harbourfront can be financed in perpetuity.
In other words, sell public parkland to developers. Let them make hundreds of millions of dollars building luxury condominiums or luxury hotels on the waterfront. The revenue from the sale of this land will go into a little trust fund and the interest, whether 10,11 or 12 per cent a year, will be used to carry on these very worth-while activities, including children's summer camp, summer festivals and book reading.
The responsibility to provide those programs is the responsibility of government, whether it is the federal government, the provincial government or the two municipal governments; the city of Toronto and metropolitan Toronto.
It is penny wise and pound foolish for the government to be selling assets in order to create trust funds in order to carry on certain activities.
If one were to advance this type of philosophy or logic on the part of the Government of Canada, then why does it not sell the House of Commons? Why does it not sell the lawn in front of the Peace Tower to private interests? One would have all kinds of private business interested in securing the rights to the lawn in front of the House of Commons.
We can still have the right to debate in the Chamber, but the money could be used in order to pay for MP's salaries or expenses. It is nonsense and it ought not to be done. We should not be selling public land or parkland in order to finance programs. I would hope that this government will realize the terrible mistake it is making. It may think that it has a short-term solution to the problems at Harbourfront. It does not want to continue funding the activities at Harbourfront.
Future generations, our children and our grandchildren, will look back to the decision of this particular Conservative government and say: "What absolute and utter nonsense, what stupidity for the government 20 or 30 years ago to sell public land on the waterfront in metropolitan Toronto to private interests". It just does not make any sense at all. That land should be developed

as parkland. It should remain in public hands. The waterfront is for the people of metropolitan Toronto, the people of Ontario and the people of Canada and it should be developed as such.

Mr. Speaker, we rise today to talk about friends of the Conservative government at the trough. This has been done constantly since 1984. We remember what the Prime Minister said during the campaign of 1984: "No other appointments will be done until every breathing and living Tory has been appointed".
Who the Tories do not appoint through different agencies they tend to take care of themselves. We have clearly seen Huang Danczkay at the airport in Toronto. The name Huang Danczkay comes up again when we talk about the waterfront.
This government wants to do away with a beautiful small property that is left in downtown Toronto. It wants to sell it like it has sold other things to its rich friends, people who come to the trough. What are we going to see? We are going to see condominiums 20 and 30 storeys high blocking the view of the average person in Toronto going to the lake, even though it is polluted.
I notice that my friends from the NDP are not here to listen to this. During the provincial campaign all sorts of promises were made about how this was going to be taken care of. It has not happened.
I want to go back in history and talk about Route Canada. I notice that the Minister of State for Multicul-turalism and Citizenship is here and he is taking a great interest and taking notes. I also will try to tell him that what this government has done is an injustice to the Canadian public. It is an injustice to all of us and to our children.
CN Express was sold for roughly $29 million in 1985-86. It was turned into Route Canada. The person who bought CN Express could not even get a credit card and yet we gave him part of Canada. He went running to the bank. He said: "Mr. friendly banker, I've got this white elephant that the government is giving me. How much money will you give me?" The bank looks at the deal and says: "Oh, it's a good deal. We're going to give you $50 million". He used that money. He bought Jaguars and he financed telephones and fax machines in its cars in the middle eighties. That was unheard of.
There was a deal struck between Route Canada buyers and the Canadian government which said that the employees of Route Canada should be kept on for three years. Eighteen months later that agreement was no longer valid. When the government was asked to open all the books and show what it has done, it found all kinds of excuses. One minister said: "I was not in power then. It was this minister". Like usual, we shuffle the deck, we have musical chairs of cabinet ministers and there is no responsibility as we clearly saw a couple of days ago in the Al-Mashat case.
Then came Air Canada. The Minister for International Trade said: "It's going to be a great deal to privatize this. It is going to be a great deal". The Canadian public was saying no. Did the government across the way listen? It was deaf. There was nothing there for it. It had ear plugs on and it was not even paying attention. The results: just a couple of months after this was taking place, 2,900 jobs were lost; VIA cutbacks and the list goes on and on and on. Now Harbourfront. Where will it end?
Some people say the Liberal Party is not for privatization. If it is a fair value market, if we are going to put what this land is worth on the table and if we are going to get a fair market value, then everybody in this House will support privatization. The government across the way is doing a gross injustice to the Canadian public. Time after time the Canadian public is raped, by either careless mistakes or intentional doings of this government.
I would not doubt for a single minute that we are going to have a fire sale in the next couple of months and this government is going to put right outside this House: "Fire sale. Our national parks are up for sale".
Do you know what is going to happen? When we go to visit our national parks there will be somebody at the toll booth and he is going to say: "It is $30 or $40 for you to get in. Canadian public, we are going to take you to the cleaners".
"People of Canada, we want to please our friends. We want to please the people who put us here. We want to please big businesses". It was those big businesses that during the elections bought the ads and in 1988 sank millions of dollars to turn the voting public. They sank millions of dollars to tell the Canadian people that free trade was going to be good for them. We have clearly

seen that the free trade legislation, since its implementation has cost Ontario, my home province, 200,000 jobs. Where will it stop?
I want to return to the Harbourfront issue because it is very important for me, my children and the children of the three million Canadians who call the greater metropolitan Toronto area their home. Some of the members across the way might be from other parts, but when they have the opportunity to visit Toronto, one landmark they always come to see is Ontario Place, the Canadian National Exhibition, and then they see this beautiful park.

Mr. Speaker, on May 14-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry. I would just like to remind the hon. member that we are under new rules of four minutes plus two minutes from the government.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I read the rules from cover to cover.
On May 14, I put a question to the Prime Minister regarding the unemployment situation in Montreal. I referred to a recent report indicating that 25 per cent of Montrealers were on unemployment insurance or welfare.
According to the recent statistics, Montreal has the highest urban unemployment rate in Canada and the highest urban poverty rate in Canada. Despite these shocking statistics, the government, in the Speech from the Throne, promised a number of new jobs by the year 2000.
If the government is really interested in the unemployment problem, why is it setting targets for the year 2000 when the needs are in 1991?
The question I put on May 14 was why do we not have a target, an agenda or a program for creating jobs this year, in 1991, to deal with the situation in Montreal and other places in Canada where there are high unemployment rates.
Well, the Prime Minister did not answer my question, and the minister who did answer my questions gave me no answer whatsoever. He referred to a few marginal programs that the government set up in Montreal and said they were working well. How can anyone believe that sort of bumph? He says they are working well, yet there is nearly a 25 per cent combined unemployment and welfare rate in Montreal. Montreal has the highest
unemployment figures in Canada and the minister says they are working well.
Just three days later, three days after I asked that initial question, Pascal's, a business that has been a successful business in Montreal for 87 years, went bankrupt. Twenty-one stores closed and 1,600 employees lost their jobs.
This government is a government of rhetoric, of overstatement and of exaggeration. It makes such outlandish statements that nobody believes anything it says any more.
When the economy was improving in 1984, the government took full credit for all the jobs that were being created. If the government had the recipe for job creation in 1985 and 1986, if it had the formula to create jobs then, why is it not producing that recipe today?
Why is it not laying down targets and programs for job creation in 1991 when the unemployment rate is over 10 per cent in Canada and when there are more than 1 million Canadians without work? In Montreal, we have a disaster zone.
If the government was really responsible and if it really had the answers and formulas for job creation, it would carry them out. The government would put them forward.
I will repeat my question. It is a simple one. Instead of a timetable for jobs for the year 2000-and I am not opposed to a timetable for jobs for the year 2000-why does it not give us a timetable for jobs for the year 1991?
I do not want an answer to some question that I have not asked at all. I will warn the public observing this debate that I will probably get some parliamentary secretary giving me an answer that was prepared by some civil servant somewhere that will have nothing to do with my question, confirming my point that this is a government of nonsense.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace said, he is indeed being answered by a parliamentary secretary, but I will try to give him as logical an answer as possible that will deal with his concerns.
May 23, 1991

Mr. Speaker, our government has set up and implemented many medium- and long-term strategies to stimulate Montreal's economy and thus the economy of Quebec. Further to the CRESSOM report, Employment and Immigration Canada will contribute $32.5 million over the next five years to help community groups and municipal bodies find long-term solutions for the problems of restructuring Montreal's disadvantaged neighbourhoods.
In the field of training, Mr. Speaker, Employment and Immigration Canada spent $2 million in November 1990 to set up a petrochemical training centre in eastern Montreal. We are answering the call of the petrochemical industry, which needs skilled workers.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace that Montreal will receive its fair share of a new labour force development strategy that increases by $800 million the funds to train the unemployed, welfare recipients, older workers and young people. Furthermore, the jobs strategy programs help nearly 8,000 individuals. In 1990-91, $32 million was spent on training programs in Montreal.
I would also like to remind the hon. member that from September 1984 to April 1991, net employment increased by 96,000 in the Montreal area. Under the previous government, from 1980 to 1984, Montreal lost
4,000	jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak further on the question I posed in the House yesterday concerning the unequal treatment of women in the Public Service of Canada.
I want to repeat the basic fact that nearly half the people working for the Public Service of Canada are women. In the management category of the Public Service of Canada, they number less than 16 per cent.
Clearly, consistent discrimination is at work to recognize people for promotion based not on what they can do but what the shape of their body is. The same barriers apply to people of visible minorities, aboriginal Canadians and people with disabilities.
I am not going to focus on them. I have spoken on them often in the House, and I will again. Today, I want to focus particularly on the status of women.
Adjournment Debate
The Public Service Commission's annual report is merely the latest proof that simply setting targets to eliminate barriers to hiring advancement and promotion has failed to bring about real change.
The task force bn barriers to women in the Public Service, which reported just a year ago last month, made it absolutely clear that the reason women do not advance in the Public Service of Canada is a cultural bias against women. It is not something that employers consciously do. It is just that, particularly at the senior levels, for all their working lives they have been surrounded by managers who happened to be male. Their whole image of successful managers is seen in male terms.
The government has talked about the few women it has appointed-and I am pleased to see the improvements-through Order in Council appointments, but these are small and insignificant measures. It is what happens to women in their everyday working lives for the Government of Canada that determines whether or not they are going to be able to support their families to the same measure, whether they are going to be able to progress and succeed, using the brains and talent they have in the best interests of their country.
Others have said it better than I, but a woman pays as much for a loaf of bread as a man does. A women pays as much for her children's shoes as a man does. She does not deserve to earn only 55 cents for every dollar a man does. It is not that women in the Public Service are less educated. They happen to be better educated than males in the Public Service.
The government talks about women in the management category. Some progress has been made. It went from a little over 14 per cent last year to a little over 15 per cent this year. Out of a management category of over
4,000	people, less than 1,000 are women. That is not right and that is not just. Examining who gets promoted, who gets hired, who gets appointed, who gets the opportunity for lateral transfers to broaden their experience, clearly explains why. Less than 25 per cent of promotions were women. Less than 25 per cent of appointments from outside into the management category were women. Barely over 20 per cent of appointments within the management category were women. Less than 20 per cent of lateral transfers, which are an opportunity to broaden experience, were women.
